items.pattern_name: Block-boundary input/output budget from an end-to-end path
items.situation: A block is being implemented independently, but its interface timing must preserve a top-level launch-to-capture requirement.
items.derivation: Start with the receiving clock edge and required end-to-end budget. For a same-frequency one-cycle path, available time is approximately Tperiod - Tsetup - Tuncertainty. Subtract the estimated external launch-side delay and receiving-side delay; the remainder is the budget available to the block/interface path. At a boundary, split the remaining budget explicitly among upstream block, interconnect, and downstream block rather than assigning the entire remainder to one block. Example: if Tperiod=1.0 ns (confidence 0.95), setup=0.08 ns (0.8), and uncertainty=0.10 ns (0.75), usable budget is 0.82 ns. If upstream gets 0.25 ns (0.65) and interconnect 0.12 ns (0.6), downstream/block input gets about 0.45 ns (0.6).
items.wrong_way: Give every block a full 1.0-ns cycle as its local input/output budget. This double-counts time and can let each block close independently while the assembled path fails.
items.defense: Show the top-level path equation, the source of each allocated delay, and demonstrate that the block budgets sum back to the end-to-end requirement; revise the split when implementation data replaces early estimates.
items.signoff_risk: Too tight: unnecessary buffering, upsizing, area/power and congestion, potentially making the block harder to route. Too loose: hidden inter-block slack consumption and a top-level setup failure after integration.
items.node_era_note: At 7nm-and-below, interconnect and variation consume a larger fraction of the budget, so the wire component usually cannot be treated as a small afterthought.

items.pattern_name: Use a virtual clock when the external timing reference is not an on-chip clock port
items.situation: An IO interface is timed by an external clock or board-level reference whose waveform should be modeled independently of the clocks physically present in the block.
items.derivation: Create a clock representing the external timing reference, then derive input delay as the time from the external launch edge to arrival at the chip boundary and output delay as the time the external receiver requires between the chip boundary and its capture edge. For setup, the rough relationship is external period minus input_delay_max minus output_delay_max minus internal setup/uncertainty. Example: external period 2.0 ns (confidence 0.95), input delay 0.55 ns (0.8), output requirement 0.65 ns (0.8), leaving roughly 0.80 ns before internal setup/uncertainty.
items.wrong_way: Tie IO delays to an arbitrary internal clock simply because that clock exists. This silently couples board timing to an implementation clock and can change the constraint when the internal clock topology changes.
items.defense: Provide the interface timing diagram or external specification showing which edge launches and captures the data, then show that the virtual-clock waveform and min/max IO delays reproduce those edges.
items.signoff_risk: Too tight: unnecessary IO optimization and possibly impossible internal timing. Too loose: the chip may meet internal STA while violating the actual board/device setup or hold requirement.
items.node_era_note: The derivation is essentially node-independent; newer nodes make package/board and on-die variation more important but do not change the virtual-clock concept.

items.pattern_name: False path versus multicycle path from functional protocol
items.situation: A path is reported as violating timing, but architectural knowledge says either the endpoints never functionally communicate under the relevant mode or they communicate only after multiple cycles.
items.derivation: First establish the protocol, not the desired STA result. If no legal operating sequence can ever require the endpoint transfer, cut it as false. If a legal sequence does require the transfer but guarantees N capture cycles, constrain setup to N cycles and adjust the hold relationship accordingly; the conventional synchronous MCP relationship is setup=N and hold=N-1. Example: for N=3 cycles (confidence 0.95), setup is checked at the third capture edge and the corresponding hold adjustment is 2 cycles (0.9).
items.wrong_way: Use a false path merely because the path is difficult, or use a multicycle exception when the transfer is actually never functionally active. The first masks a real silicon failure; the second can impose needless optimization and obscure the architectural intent.
items.defense: Attach the exception to a protocol assertion, mode/state-machine condition, or architectural timing guarantee and demonstrate that the path classification is true in every signoff-relevant mode.
items.signoff_risk: Too tight: false violations and wasted implementation effort. Too loose: real functional paths can be completely removed from timing analysis or given more cycles than the protocol actually allows.
items.node_era_note: The logical distinction is unchanged; at advanced nodes, larger variation/SI margins make incorrectly relaxed exceptions particularly dangerous.

items.pattern_name: CDC constraint follows the synchronizer architecture, not the apparent clock relationship
items.situation: Signals cross between clocks that are asynchronous or have no guaranteed phase relationship.
items.derivation: Identify the actual CDC circuit first. For a conventional synchronizer, STA should not attempt to prove a deterministic setup relationship between unrelated source and destination clocks; the CDC methodology separately checks synchronizer structure and metastability handling. If the domains are genuinely asynchronous, constrain the inter-domain timing relationship accordingly. If there is a guaranteed rational-frequency relationship, do not automatically classify it as asynchronous; derive the actual launch/capture edge relationships instead.
items.wrong_way: False-path every path whose clock names differ. This can hide a genuinely synchronous or mesochronous interface and can also conceal an incorrectly implemented CDC.
items.defense: Point to the clock-generation specification and CDC structure, then show that the exception covers exactly the intended crossing and that a separate CDC check verifies synchronizer correctness.
items.signoff_risk: Too tight: implementation may waste effort optimizing physically meaningless cross-domain timing. Too loose: an incorrectly false-pathed synchronous relationship can ship with an actual timing failure.
items.node_era_note: At 7nm-and-below, CDC metastability and variation remain architectural concerns; tighter timing makes accidental synchronous assumptions less forgiving.

items.pattern_name: Budget two unimplemented blocks by solving for complementary interface requirements
items.situation: Two blocks are being developed independently and neither has final physical timing, but the top-level path must close after integration.
items.derivation: Start from the top-level launch-to-capture requirement. Estimate block A internal delay, block B internal delay, and interconnect delay. The sum must satisfy T_A + T_wire + T_B <= T_available. Allocate a provisional interface budget to A and B so their budgets plus wire allowance equal T_available. If A is allocated 0.35 ns (confidence 0.6), wire 0.15 ns (0.6), and B 0.30 ns (0.6), their total is 0.80 ns; if the available post-uncertainty/setup budget is 0.80 ns (0.75), there is no hidden slack. The allocation can then be iterated from actual implementation data.
items.wrong_way: Give both teams the historical 'typical' budget or let each team assume the other side will absorb its residual delay. Integration then discovers that the sum of individually passing budgets exceeds the top-level budget.
items.defense: Maintain a single interface-budget ledger whose entries sum to the top-level requirement and record which estimates are measured versus assumed.
items.signoff_risk: Too tight: both blocks over-optimize their interfaces and may create excessive power/congestion. Too loose: integration exposes an impossible combined path with no remaining place to recover timing.
items.node_era_note: Advanced-node budgets tend to reserve more explicitly for physical interconnect and variation because wire delay is less predictable from logical hierarchy alone.

items.pattern_name: Early implementation over-constraint followed by evidence-based relaxation
items.situation: Placement and synthesis are immature and the engineer wants implementation to converge toward a target without yet having reliable post-route parasitics.
items.derivation: Use a deliberately conservative early target, but distinguish that target from the eventual signoff requirement. Start from the real signoff period and add an explicitly documented optimization margin rather than silently changing the specification. Example: signoff period 1.00 ns (confidence 0.95) with a provisional 5% optimization margin (confidence 0.55) gives an early target of 0.95 ns. As CTS, extraction, and variation data arrive, remove the provisional margin if the implementation has demonstrated adequate robustness.
items.wrong_way: Leave the artificial early margin in the signoff SDC, or continually tighten it because 'more negative slack means the tool works harder.' This can consume power/area and create congestion without improving real signoff quality.
items.defense: Record the mathematical relationship between the implementation target and signoff target, its intended expiration point, and the measured closure evidence that permits relaxation.
items.signoff_risk: Too tight: over-buffering, upsizing, routing congestion and power. Too loose: insufficient optimization and a late signoff timing cliff.
items.node_era_note: At 7nm-and-below, arbitrary percentage margins are less defensible because variation, SI, and extraction effects are large; measured physical uncertainty is preferable.

items.pattern_name: Generated clock derived from the actual clock-generation topology
items.situation: A register bank is clocked by a divided, multiplied, phase-shifted, or otherwise derived clock.
items.derivation: Trace the generated-clock source to the actual generating pin and derive the waveform from the transformation. For an ideal divide-by-N clock, period is approximately N times the source period; for a multiply-by-M relationship, the period is approximately source_period/M. Example: a divide-by-2 clock from a 1.0-ns source (confidence 0.95) has an ideal 2.0-ns period (0.95), subject to the actual generated waveform and source latency.
items.wrong_way: Create an unrelated primary clock with the expected period on the generated-clock net. This can lose the source relationship, phase relationship, and propagated clock behavior, producing incorrect timing between source and generated domains.
items.defense: Show the RTL/netlist clock-generation element and verify the generated waveform against simulation or the clock-generation specification; check that the generated clock reaches every intended sink.
items.signoff_risk: Too tight: false violations caused by a wrong phase or period. Too loose: real source-to-generated-clock timing failures can disappear because STA has been given the wrong relationship.
items.node_era_note: The clock relationship itself is node-independent; advanced nodes make propagated latency, uncertainty, and duty-cycle distortion more consequential.

items.pattern_name: Asynchronous interface constrained by explicit interface protocol rather than arbitrary cycle timing
items.situation: An interface has no guaranteed synchronous launch/capture relationship, such as an asynchronous handshake or externally acknowledged transfer.
items.derivation: First determine what the protocol actually guarantees: event ordering, minimum pulse width, handshake latency, or maximum response time. Do not invent a clock-period requirement. If the interface specification guarantees a maximum combinational response of D, constrain that observable requirement with an appropriate max-delay-style requirement; separately constrain minimum pulse/hold requirements where applicable. If no deterministic timing requirement exists, use structural/protocol verification rather than manufacturing a synchronous SDC relationship.
items.wrong_way: Attach the interface to the nearest system clock and assign a one-cycle input/output budget. That creates a fake timing contract and can either over-constrain implementation or falsely certify an interface whose real correctness depends on protocol behavior.
items.defense: Cite the interface protocol and show exactly which measurable timing property the SDC represents; anything not guaranteed by the protocol stays outside that timing model and is checked by the appropriate functional/interface verification.
items.signoff_risk: Too tight: needless optimization against a requirement the interface never promised. Too loose: an actual externally visible latency or pulse-width requirement may be absent from signoff.
items.node_era_note: The methodology is node-independent; advanced nodes make asynchronous control signals more vulnerable to pulse-shaping and physical variation, increasing the value of explicit protocol checks.

items.pattern_name: Separate max and min IO budgets from the same external timing diagram
items.situation: An interface has both setup and hold requirements and the external device/board consumes different amounts of time before and after the reference edge.
items.derivation: Derive max and min independently from the external launch/capture timing. For an input, input_delay_max represents latest external arrival and input_delay_min earliest arrival. For an output, output_delay_max represents the external receiver's setup requirement and output_delay_min represents its hold requirement. Do not infer min from max. Example: if external input arrival is guaranteed between 0.20 ns and 0.65 ns after the reference edge (both numbers confidence 0.85), use approximately 0.20 ns for min and 0.65 ns for max; they describe different physical cases.
items.wrong_way: Specify only max delay and assume hold will take care of itself, or derive min as max minus an arbitrary margin. This can leave hold unconstrained or create a fictitious hold requirement.
items.defense: Draw earliest and latest launch/arrival/capture edges and derive each number independently from the external component and board specification.
items.signoff_risk: Too tight: unnecessary hold/setup buffering and IO optimization. Too loose: either setup or hold can fail at the package/board/device interface despite clean internal STA.
items.node_era_note: The derivation is node-independent, although advanced-node clock/data variation and package effects make independent min/max modeling more important.

items.pattern_name: Constraint ownership at a block boundary prevents double budgeting
items.situation: Multiple teams own adjacent blocks and the same physical interconnect must be represented consistently in their SDCs.
items.derivation: Choose a single ownership convention for each delay component. For a path A→wire→B, define T_total = T_A + T_wire + T_B. Assign each term to exactly one owner. If T_total available is 0.90 ns (confidence 0.8), and provisional A/wire/B allocations are 0.35/0.20/0.35 ns (each confidence 0.6), they sum exactly to 0.90 ns. The receiving block's input delay must represent only the externally owned portion, not the same wire delay already included in its internal budget.
items.wrong_way: Both blocks include the same interface-wire allowance, or neither includes it. The former creates artificial pessimism; the latter creates a hidden integration timing deficit.
items.defense: Maintain a boundary timing contract stating who owns launch delay, wire delay, capture delay, uncertainty, and exceptions, then verify that composing the two block SDCs reproduces the top-level path requirement.
items.signoff_risk: Too tight: duplicated pessimism can force needless optimization and make independent blocks appear impossible to close. Too loose: omitted ownership creates a last-minute top-level failure.
items.node_era_note: At 7nm-and-below, explicit wire/variation ownership is more important because interconnect and context-dependent effects can dominate the boundary budget.

items.pattern_name: Block-boundary input delay budget (input-to-register)
items.situation: When assigning a maximum input delay (setup) from a chip pin to the first register inside the block, given an external launch clock and a board/interconnect delay.
items.derivation: Assume external clock period T = 10ns. External launch path delay from chip pin to external register clock is Lc = 0.5ns (assumed, conf 0.7). Board trace delay from external register to our pin is Bd = 0.8ns (assumed, conf 0.6). Our internal clock skew (clock uncertainty) is U = 0.2ns. We reserve a derate/margin of 15% of T for process variation on the external side: M = 1.5ns (assumed, conf 0.5). The input delay (max) = T - (Lc + Bd + U + M)? Actually, standard equation: external clock path to launch register + board delay + our internal clock path skew. The official SDC set_input_delay -max = (external launch clock path delay + board trace delay) - (external capture clock path delay). We usually simplify: set_input_delay -max = (1 - alpha) * T, where alpha is the fraction of cycle available for internal logic. We choose alpha = 0.6, so input delay = 0.4 * T = 4.0ns. Then internal logic has 6.0ns to meet. Derivation: we measure external board timing and clock jitter, then back-calculate: input_delay = T - (internal_path_required_time). We compute required internal path = T - board_delay - clock_uncertainty - margin. So input_delay = board_delay + clock_uncertainty + margin. Here we set input_delay = 4.0ns (board+margin+uncertainty).
items.wrong_way: Using the chip pin's own output driver delay as the input delay, or setting it to zero because 'the board is short' – this silently forces the internal logic to run at full cycle minus zero, leaving no time for the external launch path, causing hidden timing violations at the top level that require massive respin.
items.defense: Present the external timing budget document from system engineering: measured or simulated board trace delays, clock source jitter, and the allowed internal logic time. Show that the internal logic has at least 60% of the cycle, which is validated by a timing-closure histogram of the first registers.
items.signoff_risk: Too tight (input delay too large): internal logic is over-constrained, causing over-optimization, area/power blowup, and possible routing congestion; too loose (input delay too small): top-level integration fails with setup violations at the pins that cannot be fixed without board re-spin.
items.node_era_note: At 7nm, board-level interconnect OCV is smaller but on-chip variation (OCV) is larger, so we add a separate on-chip derate to the internal path; at 28nm, board delay dominates.

items.pattern_name: Block-boundary output delay budget (register-to-output)
items.situation: When assigning a maximum output delay (setup) from the last register inside the block to an external chip pin, given a capture clock at an external register.
items.derivation: Given period T = 10ns. External capture clock path to the external register is Ccapture = 0.6ns (assumed, conf 0.6). Board trace from our pin to the external register is B = 1.2ns (assumed, conf 0.7). Our internal clock skew to the launching register is U = 0.15ns. We reserve a margin of 10% of T for external variation M = 1.0ns (assumed, conf 0.5). The output delay (max) = T - (Ccapture + B + U + M) ? Actually, the standard is: set_output_delay -max = (external capture clock path + board delay) - (external launch clock path) but we typically set it as the time allowed from our launch clock to the pin, so we compute: output_delay = T - (time available for external logic). We set output_delay = T - (Ccapture + B + margin) = 10 - (0.6+1.2+1.0) = 7.2ns? That would mean our internal path gets only 2.8ns, which is too tight. Actually, we set output_delay so that our internal logic can take a fraction of T. We choose output_delay = 0.35*T = 3.5ns, leaving internal logic 6.5ns. The arithmetic: we measure board + external capture = 1.8ns, plus margin = 1.0ns, so total external overhead = 2.8ns. Then output_delay = external overhead + some guard = 3.5ns, meaning we allocate 3.5ns for the external path, leaving 6.5ns for internal path. Derivation step: output_delay = (board_delay + capture_clock_delay + margin) * 1.1 (safety factor).
items.wrong_way: Setting output delay to zero or to the Tclk-to-Q of the last flop, because you think the external capture is instantaneous – this silently hides that the board and external clock path consume almost half the cycle, causing top-level hold violations that are impossible to fix because the internal data arrives too early.
items.defense: Provide the system-level interface spec showing the external capture clock phase and board propagation. Show that the combined external path (board + capture skew) is under 3.5ns, which is the budget we allocated.
items.signoff_risk: Too tight (output delay too high): internal logic is over-tightened, may fail to close within block; too loose (output delay too low): external setup violations at top level, requiring board delay reduction or higher drive strength.
items.node_era_note: At 7nm, the output delay is often limited by package parasitics and the external capture clock is more predictable due to improved PLL jitter; at 28nm, board traces dominate.

items.pattern_name: False path vs multicycle path on non-critical combinatorial logic
items.situation: A data path between two flops has a large logic depth that cannot meet the clock period, but the signal is not timing-critical (e.g., a status register updated infrequently).
items.derivation: Check the functional specification: the path is enabled by a write enable that asserts only once every N cycles. We set a multicycle path with N=2 (or 3). Derivation: we compute the worst-case delay of the combinational cloud, say 12ns, while period is 5ns. We set multicycle setup = 3 (i.e., 3 cycles) so the capture flop uses launch edge 3 cycles earlier. We do not set multicycle hold, or we set hold=2 to avoid hold violation on the launch edge. We derive the number M = ceil(delay / period) + 1 margin. For delay=12ns, period=5ns, M=ceil(12/5)+1 = 3+1? Actually, we use M=3 (capture on the 3rd edge). We verify that the path is not a feedback path that would affect next state incorrectly.
items.wrong_way: Setting a false path instead of multicycle because it's 'not used often' – this can break the path if the enable is ever asserted on consecutive cycles (e.g., due to a burst), leading to functional corruption that is extremely difficult to debug.
items.defense: Show the RTL that the enable signal is a one-hot pulse that repeats every 4 cycles minimum. Also show the timing report that the path has 12ns delay, and we have 3 cycles = 15ns budget, so it's safe. The design review signs off on the functional correctness of the delayed capture.
items.signoff_risk: Too tight (using false path or 1-cycle): the path will not close, causing massive logic restructuring. Too loose (using too many cycles): area blow-up due to extra pipeline stages if we relax, but if using multicycle constraint without changing RTL, it's a functional risk – if the enable frequency increases, data is read too late, causing data corruption.
items.node_era_note: At 7nm, multicycle paths are more common due to higher wire delays; we often use multicycle setup = 2 and hold = 1 as a default for cross-hierarchy routes.

items.pattern_name: CDC constraint for asynchronous dual-flop synchronizer (setup/hold exemptions)
items.situation: A signal crosses a clock-domain boundary where the two clocks are asynchronous (no known phase relationship).
items.derivation: We identify the synchronizer: two flops back-to-back in the destination domain, with no combinatorial logic between them. We set `set_clock_groups -asynchronous` between the two clocks, which removes all timing paths between them. However, we must explicitly set a false path from the source flop to the first synchronizer flop (since it's timing-critical only for metastability, not setup/hold). We derive that we need to add a `set_max_delay -from src_clk -to dst_clk`? No, we set `set_false_path -from [get_clocks src] -to [get_clocks dst]`. Then we add a `set_clock_uncertainty` on the synchronizer’s first flop to ensure metastability margin (sometimes not needed if the library provides metastability-robust flops). We also set a `set_multicycle_path -setup 2 -hold 1` from the first synchronizer flop to the second to allow an extra cycle for settling (if the clocks are slow). Derivation: we look at the synchronizer's required MTBF; we ensure the data toggle is slow enough (e.g., < 1/10 of the dst clock) by constraining the source logic to produce stable data for at least two dst cycles.
items.wrong_way: Simply applying `set_false_path` on all cross-domain paths without the explicit multicycle for the synchronizer stages, leading to the timing analyzer ignoring the settling time, which may allow the second flop to capture metastable data, causing functional failures.
items.defense: Show the CDC document that lists all synchronizers. Show that the source flop to first dst flop has a false path, and the first-to-second flop has a multicycle setup=2 to guarantee metastability settling. Also show that the source data is stable for at least 2 cycles of the destination clock (by constraining the source toggling rate).
items.signoff_risk: Too tight (no false path, or single-cycle path): massive timing violations at CDC crossing, impossible to close, may force adding more pipeline stages. Too loose (false path without any timing constraint): the synchronizer may not have enough time to settle if the source data changes too fast, causing intermittent failures that are impossible to reproduce.
items.node_era_note: At 7nm, we often use a third flop (three-stage synchronizer) for high-speed interfaces, and we set multicycle setup=3, hold=2; at 28nm, two flops suffice.

items.pattern_name: Budgeting between two unbuilt blocks (top-down split)
items.situation: At the early chip planning stage, the top-level period T is known, but two blocks (Block A and Block B) are not yet implemented. The interconnect between them is fixed, and we need to split the available time between internal logic of A, the interconnect, and internal logic of B.
items.derivation: Total period T = 10ns. Fixed interconnect delay between blocks (estimated from floorplan) = 2.0ns (assumed, conf 0.6). We reserve 10% of T for clock skew and margin = 1.0ns (assumed, conf 0.5). Remaining time for logic = T - interconnect - skew = 10 - 2 - 1 = 7ns. We split this 7ns between A and B based on their estimated logic depth: if A has roughly twice the logic of B, we give A 4.7ns and B 2.3ns. Derivation: we compute gate counts or estimated stage delays from previous designs. We set `set_input_delay` and `set_output_delay` for each block accordingly. For example, for Block A output to Block B input: we set output delay of A = interconnect + time_allocated_for_B? Actually, if we are constraining A's output to the top-level pin, we include the interconnect plus B's input budget. So we set set_output_delay -max = (interconnect + B_internal_budget) = 2.0 + 2.3 = 4.3ns from A's clock. For B, set_input_delay -max = interconnect + A_internal_budget = 2.0 + 4.7 = 6.7ns? That would exceed 10? Wait, we need consistency: A_launch + A_internal + interconnect + B_internal + B_capture_skew = T. We define A_internal = 4.7, B_internal = 2.3, interconnect = 2.0, skew=1.0. Then 4.7+2.3+2.0+1.0=10.0. So for A's output delay (time from A clock to A pin), we set it to A_internal + interconnect? Actually, set_output_delay from A is the time from A clock to the input of B's flop, but it's relative to B's clock. The typical derivation: set_output_delay -max (from A) = (interconnect + B_internal_budget + B_clock_uncertainty) - (A_clock_uncertainty) ... we simplify by distributing the skew. We just allocate explicit numbers and back-annotate.
items.wrong_way: Splitting the period equally (50/50) without considering the actual logic depth, or ignoring the interconnect and assuming it can be pipelined later, causing both blocks to over-optimize one and under-optimize the other, resulting in a late respin to repartition.
items.defense: Show a spreadsheet of estimated gate-level delays per block, derived from RTL synthesis on a reference technology. Show floorplan wire lengths and resistance-capacitance extraction for the interconnect. The split is reviewed by the block owners and adjusted based on their confidence.
items.signoff_risk: Too tight on one block: that block fails to close, requiring interface repartition; too loose on the other: the top-level period is still met but the tight block may have to use higher Vt or larger buffers, increasing power.
items.node_era_note: At 7nm, interconnect delay is much more variable, so we allocate a larger uncertainty margin (up to 20%) and use statistical budgeting; at 28nm, we use fixed RC estimates.

items.pattern_name: Over-constraining strategy (aggressive early target) and relaxation phase
items.situation: During early RTL synthesis and placement, the clock period is not yet tight; we set a more aggressive (shorter) period to push the tools to optimize, with a plan to relax later.
items.derivation: Given final target T_final = 10ns. We set an over-constrained period T_early = 0.85 * T_final = 8.5ns (assumed, conf 0.7). We also tighten all input/output delays proportionally. The derivation is based on historical data that the tools lose 10-20% performance after clock tree insertion and routing. We set a linear scaling factor = 0.85. We also set a more aggressive clock uncertainty (e.g., 0.2ns vs 0.5ns) to force better placement. We plan to relax to 10ns at the post-CTS stage by adjusting the SDC to T_final and increasing uncertainty to actual values.
items.wrong_way: Keeping the over-constrained target throughout the flow, because you think it will 'ensure margins,' which causes excessive area, power, and route congestion, and often makes the design unroutable because the tool tries too hard to optimize impossible paths.
items.defense: Show a graph of slack degradation over the flow from previous projects, proving that 85% is a safe overdrive that does not blow up area. Also show that the design meets 8.5ns in synthesis with reasonable area, so we have margin.
items.signoff_risk: Too tight (e.g., 70%): tools may fail to converge, causing endless loops; too loose (e.g., 95%): when the real degradation hits, the design fails at signoff, forcing a last-minute constraint relaxation that may not be enough.
items.node_era_note: At 7nm, the degradation from synthesis to route is larger (up to 25%), so we use 0.75 factor; at 28nm, 0.85 is typical.

items.pattern_name: Virtual clock for board-level input/output (IO) timing
items.situation: The chip interfaces with an external device that has its own clock, which is not the same as the chip's internal PLL clock. We need to model that external clock as a virtual clock for IO constraints.
items.derivation: We define a virtual clock `virt_clk` with the same period as the external device's clock (e.g., 20ns) and a defined waveform (e.g., rising at 0ns). We then set `set_input_delay -clock virt_clk -max` and `set_output_delay -clock virt_clk -max` for all IO ports. The derivation: we measure the external clock skew between the external device and our chip – say the external clock arrives at our chip pin with a delay of 1.5ns relative to the virtual clock (assumed, conf 0.6). For input, we set input_delay = external_clock_to_pin + board_trace_to_pin + external_device_clock_to_data. We sum them: e.g., 2.0ns external device launch, 0.8ns board trace, so input_delay = 2.8ns. For output, we set output_delay = board_trace + external_device_setup_time. We assume external device setup = 1.0ns, board=0.8ns, so output_delay = 1.8ns.
items.wrong_way: Using the chip's internal clock for IO constraints without a virtual clock, assuming the external clock is the same as internal, which ignores the phase and frequency difference, causing unrealistic timing that fails when the external clock is out of phase.
items.defense: Provide the external device datasheet and the board delay analysis. Show that the virtual clock waveform matches the external device's clock signal as measured on the PCB. Show that we have a board-level timing simulation that validates these values.
items.signoff_risk: Too tight (input/output delays too large): internal logic is over-constrained, may fail; too loose: external device sees setup/hold violations, causing system failure.
items.node_era_note: At 7nm, virtual clocks are often used with double-data-rate constraints and require exact duty-cycle modeling; at 28nm, single-edge is common.

items.pattern_name: Generated clock (divide-by-2 with phase shift) constraint
items.situation: A clock divider flop produces a divided clock (e.g., half frequency) that is used as a clock for a large portion of the design, often with a known phase relationship.
items.derivation: Assume master clock `clk` period = 5ns. The divider flop toggles on the rising edge of `clk`. The divided output `div_clk` has period 10ns, rising at 5ns and falling at 10ns? Actually, if toggles at 0,5,10, the rising edge of div_clk is at 0ns, then falling at 5ns, rising again at 10ns – so it's a 50% duty cycle with period 10ns. We use `create_generated_clock -name div_clk -source [get_pins clk] -divide_by 2 -master_clock clk`. The tool automatically derives the waveform. If we need a specific phase (e.g., rising edge at 2.5ns), we use `-edges {1 3 5}`. Derivation: we set the divide-by factor, and the tool computes the edges. We also need to set `set_clock_groups -physically_exclusive` if the master and divided clocks never interact, but often they do (data crosses from fast to slow), so we set a multicycle path.
items.wrong_way: Defining the divided clock as a separate unrelated clock with its own period, ignoring the phase relationship, which breaks the timing analysis at the cross-over because the tool will not know they are synchronous, leading to unsafe false paths or missing timing checks.
items.defense: Show the RTL divider circuit and the timing diagram. The generated clock declaration is consistent with the edge flop's toggle. The tool's derived latency is verified by checking the arrival time at the clock pins of the flops in the divided domain.
items.signoff_risk: Too tight (if defined as unrelated): cross-domain paths may be incorrectly timed or false, causing either missing violations or false violations. Too loose (if defined correctly but with incorrect phase): the crossover paths have wrong slack, causing signoff failure when the phase is mis-specified.
items.node_era_note: At 7nm, generated clocks are often used for multiple frequency domains and require careful duty-cycle variation due to on-chip variation; at 28nm, divide-by-2 is straightforward.

items.pattern_name: Asynchronous interface handshake (req/ack) with no clock relation
items.situation: An interface uses a request-acknowledge handshake where the request is sent from one clock domain and the acknowledge comes back, without a fixed clock ratio. The path between the two is purely combinatorial, and we need to ignore timing.
items.derivation: We identify that the handshake signals are synchronized via dual-flop synchronizers in both directions. However, there is also a combinatorial path from the source flop of the req to the destination flop of the ack? Actually, the req path is synchronized, the ack path is synchronized. The timing between the source req flop (in src domain) and the dest ack flop (in src domain) might have a combinatorial path? Often, the source sends req, waits for ack, which goes through synchronizers. The path from req to ack is usually asynchronous and we set `set_false_path -from [get_clocks src] -to [get_clocks src]` for the combinational logic that combines ack? Actually, we set false path on the asynchronous handshake logic because it is not cycle-accurate – it is sampled only when stable. Derivation: we set `set_clock_groups -asynchronous` between the two clocks, and then set `set_false_path` on all paths that are purely combinatorial between the synchronizer outputs and the state machine logic that interprets the ack, because the state machine is designed to wait for a stable ack.
items.wrong_way: Trying to constrain the handshake with a multicycle path based on the ratio of clocks, which breaks if the clocks are not frequency-locked, causing functional failures when the ack arrives at an unpredictable time.
items.defense: Show the RTL state machine that does not sample the ack until it is stable for at least two cycles of the source clock. The false path is justified because the timing of the ack arrival does not affect the next state transition – it only enables the transition after a period of waiting.
items.signoff_risk: Too tight (no false path, trying to time it): the path will have huge violations because the crossing is truly asynchronous. Too loose (false path everywhere, but missing the metastability constraints): could miss a setup violation on the synchronizer flops, which are actually critical for metastability.
items.node_era_note: At 7nm, we often use a four-phase handshake with additional timing constraints on the synchronizer delays; at 28nm, simple false path suffices.

items.pattern_name: Clock-gating check (enable path) timing constraint
items.situation: An integrated clock-gating cell (ICG) uses an enable signal that must be stable around the clock edge to avoid glitches. We need to constrain the enable path relative to the clock.
items.derivation: ICG has a setup and hold requirement on the enable pin relative to the clock. We derive the `set_clock_gating_check -setup 0.5ns -hold 0.3ns` (values from library, assumed, conf 0.9). We also need to ensure that the enable arrives in time. We derive the maximum delay from the source flop to the enable pin: it must be less than (T - ICG_setup - skew - margin). We set a multicycle path on the enable? Actually, we use `set_clock_gating_check -setup` and let the tool time it. We derive the allowable enable delay by subtracting the ICG setup from the half-cycle or full-cycle depending on latch type. For a latch-based ICG, the enable must be stable before the falling edge of the clock for a negative latch. We set `set_clock_gating_check -setup [expr 0.4*T]` if the enable is generated from the same clock.
items.wrong_way: Assuming the enable is always stable and not timing it, which can lead to glitches on the clock, causing functional errors and timing violations that are hard to debug.
items.defense: Show the library timing arc for the ICG and demonstrate that the enable path slack is positive at all corners. Also show that the enable is registered and goes through a simple path.
items.signoff_risk: Too tight (aggressive gating check): the enable path may be over-constrained, causing large buffers; too loose (relaxed check): glitches can occur, causing race conditions.
items.node_era_note: At 7nm, ICG setup/hold are more sensitive due to lower voltage; we use tighter values and also check across all timing corners; at 28nm, default library values suffice.

items.pattern_name: Symmetric 50/50 Block Boundary IO Budgeting
items.situation: Budgeting input and output delay constraints (`set_input_delay` / `set_output_delay`) for two top-level blocks being designed concurrently before either layout or routing exists.
items.derivation: Given clock period T_clk: deduct clock uncertainty T_unc and target setup timing margin M (e.g. 10%, confidence 0.8) to get net usable period T_net = T_clk - T_unc - M. Divide T_net evenly: 50% allocated to internal block logic/reg-to-out, 50% allocated to external block in-to-reg plus top-level wire RC flight time. Thus, set_input_delay -max = T_clk - (0.5 * T_net) and set_output_delay -max = T_clk - (0.5 * T_net). For hold, budget external minimum delay as 0ns initially with explicit top-level trace delay checks deferred to post-route.
items.wrong_way: Constraining IOs with 0ns or arbitrary 80% T_clk input delays without coordinating with the partner block owner. Downstream, one block optimizer bloats logic to meet impossible 20% residual margins while the partner block wastes area by under-optimizing.
items.defense: Budget spreadsheet signed off by both block leads showing explicit T_net breakdown, clock uncertainty allocation, and assumed top-level routing layer / length limits.
items.signoff_risk: If too tight: synthetic timing violations force unnecessary logic restructuring, area bloat, or gate sizing that exacerbates local congestion. If too loose: top-level integration timing fails after full chip routing, requiring expensive late-stage ECOs.
items.node_era_note: At 28nm, a simple 50/50 period split was sufficient; at 7nm and below, top-level wire RC delay dominates, requiring reserving up to 30% of T_clk purely for top-level interconnect (confidence 0.85) before splitting the rest.

items.pattern_name: Virtual Clock Framing for System-Synchronous IO
items.situation: Constraining external off-chip input/output interfaces where the clock originates off-chip or board trace delays create a phase offset relative to the internal core clock.
items.derivation: Create an unattached virtual clock (`create_clock -name v_clk -period T_clk`). For input constraints: set_input_delay -clock v_clk -max (T_ext_launch_max + T_board_trace_max) -min (T_ext_launch_min + T_board_trace_min). For output constraints: set_output_delay -clock v_clk -max (T_ext_setup + T_board_trace_max) -min (-T_ext_hold + T_board_trace_min). This decouples internal clock tree synthesis (CTS) insertion delay adjustments from board-level absolute timing reference requirements.
items.wrong_way: Referencing the internal clock directly (`set_input_delay -clock clk_core`). When CTS builds the internal clock tree and adds 1.5ns insertion delay, the tool shifts the input setup target by 1.5ns, causing false timing violations or invalid optimizations.
items.defense: Board-level PCB layout trace length report and external device AC timing datasheet parameters explicitly mapped to `v_clk` parameters.
items.signoff_risk: If too tight: forces extreme I/O delay cell insertion or local pad logic sizing. If too loose: silicon fails AC timing specifications at the PCB boundary despite clean internal timing reports.

items.pattern_name: Validating and Defending Multicycle Paths for Handshake Protocols
items.situation: Constraining multi-cycle data paths controlled by a validated enable signal or state machine handshake (e.g., data bus stable for N clock cycles).
items.derivation: Identify data path driven by enable pulse active every N cycles (e.g. N=2). Derive setup multicycle: `set_multicycle_path 2 -setup -from [get_cells src_reg] -to [get_cells dst_reg]`. Derive hold multicycle: because setup shift implicitly moves hold capture edge forward by N-1 cycles, explicitly reset hold capture edge to launch edge via `set_multicycle_path 1 -hold -from [get_cells src_reg] -to [get_cells dst_reg]` (N-1 cycles relative to setup).
items.wrong_way: Applying `set_multicycle_path 2 -setup` without the corresponding `-hold 1` exception. Synthesis/STA engines will evaluate hold timing against cycle N-1 instead of cycle 0, causing the tool to insert massive streams of unnecessary hold buffers.
items.defense: Formal verification proof or RTL assertion proving the enable generator guarantees data stability for N cycles before capture edge, attached directly to the constraint review record.
items.signoff_risk: If too tight (or left unconstrained as 1-cycle): tool over-optimizes combinatorial logic at expense of area/power. If too loose (e.g., N set to 3 when enable allows 2): functional hold or setup race occurs in silicon, causing data corruption.

items.pattern_name: Gray-Code Bus Asynchronous Clock Domain Crossing Exception
items.situation: Constraining an asynchronous FIFO pointer or Gray-coded multi-bit bus crossing between completely asynchronous clock domains.
items.derivation: Because clocks are asynchronous, standard period-based setup/hold checks are invalid. Apply false path: `set_clock_groups -asynchronous` or `set_false_path -from [get_clocks clk_a] -to [get_clocks clk_b]`. To prevent the router from placing bits of the Gray-code bus arbitrarily far apart (which invalidates single-bit transition assumptions), add a maximum delay constraint: `set_max_delay -from [get_cells ptr_reg[*]] -to [get_cells synchronizer_reg[*]] T_dest_period` with `-ignore_clock_latency` to bound skew across bus bits (e.g., max skew <= 0.5 * T_dest_period, confidence 0.85).
items.wrong_way: Applying `set_false_path` without a corresponding `set_max_delay` or `set_bus_skew` constraint. The router treats the net as unconstrained and may route one bit across the chip, causing multi-bit transitions at the synchronizer and FIFO pointer corruption.
items.defense: CDC structural check report (e.g., SpyGlass CDC) confirming synchronizer cell presence plus STA report verifying max-delay and bus-skew constraints on CDC bits.
items.signoff_risk: If too tight: routing engine chokes trying to achieve tight absolute latency across asynchronous domains. If too loose (or false path only): pointer skew causes multi-bit transitions at receiver synchronizers, causing FIFO data corruption or system deadlock.
items.node_era_note: At 7nm and below, explicit `set_bus_skew` constraints are mandatory alongside `set_max_delay` due to large local wire variation across parallel bit tracks.

items.pattern_name: Phased Over-Constraining Derate Strategy during Synthesis/Placement
items.situation: Preventing downstream timing degradation during physical design by applying deliberate margin during early synthesis and placement steps.
items.derivation: In early synthesis/place, actual clock tree latency, wire RC, and OCV variations are unknown. Add deliberate setup clock uncertainty or clock period derate: `set_clock_uncertainty -setup U_synth clk` where U_synth = T_clk * 0.15 (15% of period, confidence 0.8). During post-CTS / detailed routing, remove the synthetic over-constraint and apply real signoff OCV/POCV derates + actual clock tree jitter/skew numbers: `set_clock_uncertainty -setup U_signoff clk` (e.g., 3-5% of period, confidence 0.85).
items.wrong_way: Applying full signoff POCV derates and final low clock uncertainty during early RTL synthesis. Synthesis produces undersized gates and tight logic depth; once routing capacitance and CTS skew appear post-layout, the design fails timing catastrophically.
items.defense: Historical floorplan correlation data showing typical timing degradation from synthesis to post-route for the given node and implementation flow.
items.signoff_risk: If too tight at signoff: design bloats in power and area trying to meet artificial margin. If too loose during synthesis: physical design cannot converge post-route without major logic restructuring.
items.node_era_note: At 28nm, a uniform 10% clock uncertainty over-constraint worked well; at 7nm and below, over-constraining must be done via tight path-based margin / distance-based wire models rather than pure global clock uncertainty to avoid tool divergence.

items.pattern_name: Synchronous Divide-by-N Generated Clock Derivation
items.situation: Constraining an internal clock generated by a flip-flop divider circuit driven by a master clock.
items.derivation: Define the generated clock on the output pin of the divider register: `create_generated_clock -name clk_div2 -source [get_pins div_reg/CP] -divide_by 2 [get_pins div_reg/Q]`. STA automatically derives phase relationship, frequency, and edge alignments relative to the master clock source pin. For setup/hold between master and generated clock, STA checks the most restrictive edge combination (e.g., launch on master at t=0ns, capture on div2 at t=T_master).
items.wrong_way: Defining the output clock using `create_clock -period (2*T_master)` instead of `create_generated_clock`. STA treats the two clocks as completely independent with unmanaged phase relationships, masking real clock-path latency and skew correlations.
items.defense: Schematic/RTL inspection showing register-based clock divider topology and STA clock-network report confirming traced source pin connection.
items.signoff_risk: If misconfigured as primary clock: STA misses phase correlation and clock tree latency sharing between master and child clocks, causing severe false setup/hold violations or masking real timing errors.

items.pattern_name: Inter-block boundary I/O budget split (input/output delay between two blocks on a shared clock)
items.situation: Two blocks not yet integrated (or one being revised) must each sign off against a boundary path; someone has to decide how the period divides between launch logic, interconnect, and capture logic.
items.derivation: 1) Fix shared-clock period T for the boundary path. 2) Reserve interconnect margin I as a fraction of T — order of 10-20% at 28nm, tightened where repeaters/latency are explicitly modeled (confidence 0.5 on the range). 3) Split the remaining (T − I) between launch logic L and capture logic C: default 50/50 when both sides are of similar depth, reweighted (e.g., 70/30 toward the deeper side) when one side is a register directly at the pin (confidence 0.5 on the 70/30 shape). 4) Charge half the interconnect to each side: on the launch block set_output_delay −max = C + I/2; on the capture block set_input_delay −max = L + I/2. Self-check: internal budget left in the launch block = T − (C + I/2) = L + I/2, which matches the capture block's assumed input budget. 5) Derive −min values so the integrated hold check covers interconnect plus capture-side hold margin; set −min near the fast-corner interconnect estimate rather than zero-by-default (confidence 0.5). 6) Exchange a budget table with the neighboring block owner before either block freezes; both sign the same table.
items.wrong_way: Setting output_delay to the full period (zero internal budget for the launch block, unclosable) or input_delay to zero (capture block must absorb everything). Subtler: forgetting the interconnect reserve — each block signs off clean and the path fails at integration by exactly the reserved margin, discovered weeks later.
items.defense: The budget table itself: both boundary reports shown side by side at review, each matching the agreed split; the split re-derived whenever either side's logic depth changes materially.
items.signoff_risk: Too tight: over-design (buffers, area) on the budgeted side, or fake failures that erode trust in the budget process. Too loose: integration failure at top level, forcing rework of a block already signed off — the most expensive failure mode in this list.
items.node_era_note: at 28nm the margin was a flat percentage of period; at 7nm-and-below budgets carry explicit source-latency and repeater terms, so pure-percentage splits under-budget long routes

items.pattern_name: Primary/IO budget via virtual clocks from external device timing
items.situation: Constraining chip-level input/output ports against an external device's datasheet timing using a clock defined with no port.
items.derivation: 1) create_clock on a virtual (portless) object with the external/system period T. 2) Input side: set_input_delay −max = external Tco(max) + board trace max; −min = external Tco(min) + board trace min (confidence 0.7 — standard common-clock formulation). 3) Output side: set_output_delay −max = external Tsu + trace max; the −min value encodes the external hold requirement adjusted by board clock skew between our clock pin and the device clock pin. Sign conventions for the −min term differ between tools' IO timing equations — verify the direction empirically: increasing −min must tighten the hold check (confidence 0.6 on the verification recipe; no universal formula quoted). 4) If the board clock is common to both chips, the clock-trace skew enters once, against the clock relationship — the classic error is double-counting it into both clock and data numbers (confidence 0.5).
items.wrong_way: Treating the IO delays as free knobs inflated until timing passes — silently exporting the failure to the board, where it appears as a system-margin problem nobody traces back to the SDC.
items.defense: The external device datasheet page and the board trace estimate attached to the constraint file header; every IO delay number traceable to one of those two documents.
items.signoff_risk: Too tight: over-design at the IO ring and fake failures on real interfaces. Too loose: the chip passes signoff but the board fails system timing, with the defect invisible in any single-chip report.
items.node_era_note: at 7nm-and-below on-die variation and derates make the min-side and corner scoping matter more, but the datasheet arithmetic shape is unchanged

items.pattern_name: False path vs multicycle adjudication (with the hold adjustment)
items.situation: A path misses timing and someone proposes an exception; the decision is whether the path legitimately takes N cycles, or is architecturally unreachable, or is neither and must be fixed.
items.derivation: 1) Find the architectural qualifier: capture flop enabled every N cycles (enable from a counter or divided clock); N = enable period / clock period. 2) set_multicycle_path N −setup on the launch→capture scope (explicit −end when clocks differ). 3) Immediately add set_multicycle_path (N−1) −hold on the same scope — without it the tool checks hold across N−1 cycles, an impossible requirement (this adjustment mechanism itself is textbook-standard; the adjudication discipline is the practice part). 4) Choose false path only when the path cannot be exercised at all: proven mutually exclusive selects, static configuration straps, or clocks already declared asynchronous. 5) Review heuristic: any proposed false path in a datapath defaults to multicycle unless a formal exclusivity argument exists; 'the path is hard to close' is never, by itself, a false-path justification.
items.wrong_way: False path used as a closure tool — the path goes unchecked and silicon fails with no signoff warning. Second classic: MPC applied without the hold adjustment, flooding signoff with impossible hold violations, whereupon someone false-paths the path to clean the report — compounding one error into a silent one.
items.defense: Waveform or RTL enable tree showing the N-cycle validity window for multicycle; exclusivity proof for any false path; the exception report showing the shifted check edges.
items.signoff_risk: Too tight (multicycle on a truly single-cycle path): real failures get N-cycle leniency they don't deserve and escape. Too loose (false path on a live path): zero coverage, silicon failure with no report ever flagging it — the worst asymmetry in constraint practice.
items.node_era_note: no-era-difference-recalled — the mechanics are node-independent; only the closure pressure that tempts false paths varies

items.pattern_name: CDC constraint package: asynchronous clock groups plus bounded crossings plus synchronizer audit
items.situation: Two or more unrelated clock domains exchange data; every crossing needs a documented synchronizer scheme and the constraints must protect, not erase, those crossings.
items.derivation: 1) Enumerate clocks; set_clock_groups −asynchronous only between pairs where EVERY crossing has a documented synchronizer. 2) Classify each crossing: 1-bit level → 2-flop sync; multi-bit counter → gray code; data bus → handshake or async FIFO. 3) Bound every crossing with set_max_delay −from [source flops] −to [first sync flop] of order one period of the faster clock (confidence 0.5 on the one-period idiom; intent is only to keep the transition from smearing across multiple receive edges), preserving gray-bus coherency and the MTBF assumptions. 4) Run a crossing audit: every path between asynchronous groups must map to the synchronizer inventory; an unmapped path is a bug in constraints or RTL — decide which, don't ignore it.
items.wrong_way: Blanket false_path or clock_groups with no max_delay bounds — gray-code counters sampled non-coherently (silent state corruption visible only in gated-delay simulation or silicon), handshakes with no stable-window enforcement, and no report anywhere that flags it.
items.defense: Synchronizer inventory table diffed against the crossing audit report; gray-code property check on the RTL; MTBF calculation for deep asynchronous paths.
items.signoff_risk: Too loose: metastability or coherency escapes to silicon — the worst post-silicon debug class there is. Too tight: fabricated max_delay failures on crossings invite engineers to strip the bounds to converge, destroying the protection at exactly the moment it matters.
items.node_era_note: at 7nm-and-below the crossing inventory is increasingly machine-checked by formal CDC tools fed from the same constraints, rather than only reviewed by hand

items.pattern_name: Generated/divided clock definition (including gated-clock outputs)
items.situation: A clock is divided by a register, split through a clock-gating cell, or produced by a PLL; the constraint must preserve the parent-child relationship.
items.derivation: 1) At each clock-splitting element, define create_generated_clock with −source at the driving clock pin and the true relationship: −divide_by N for clean dividers, an explicit −edges list for irregular duty or odd division. 2) For an integrated clock-gating cell, define the generated clock at its output pin, 1:1, source = the cell's clock input pin, so tree latency beyond the gate stays comparable with ungated sibling branches. 3) Do not declare a separate primary clock on the divided net: the generated definition keeps parent↔child paths checked (setup into the divider register, gating arcs) and keeps source latency continuous through the hierarchy. 4) Verify via the clock report that source tracing shows one root, then set latency/uncertainty on the generated clock, not the parent, for leaf budgeting.
items.wrong_way: create_clock on the divided net: parent and child become 'unrelated' clocks — parent-to-child data paths silently drop into the false/asynchronous bucket, the parent's source insertion delay never enters the child's budget, and balancing gated against ungated siblings becomes impossible.
items.defense: Clock report showing the generated relationship and traced source; divider/ICG schematic in review; the leaf latency arithmetic reconciled against the tree report.
items.signoff_risk: Too tight (extra checks from a correct generated definition): some real gating-logic arcs show up and must be handled, but nothing is silently lost. Too loose (separate primary clock): entire path classes vanish from signoff without any violation to argue about — the failure is the absence of a report.

items.pattern_name: Pre-CTS over-constraint via clock uncertainty with scheduled relaxation
items.situation: Before CTS the clock network is ideal (zero skew by default), so early implementation must inject the skew/jitter/margin that will exist later — and must later give it back.
items.derivation: 1) Pre-CTS: set_clock_uncertainty −setup U where U ≈ expected post-CTS skew + jitter + ECO residue; order of 5-10% of period or ~20-80ps depending on tree size (confidence 0.4), with ECO residue ~10-20ps (confidence 0.4). 2) Hold side: smaller uncertainty pre-route, order of expected hold-fix skew (confidence 0.35), fully replaced by real propagated skew after CTS. 3) Optional early-phase data over-constraint: tighten boundary budgets by a small fixed margin, order 5-10% of the block budget (confidence 0.4), released at integration. 4) Relaxation gates: after CTS, replace setup U with (measured skew + jitter + small residue); after route, uncertainty is jitter plus mandated signoff margin only. Every relaxation step cites the skew histogram from the stage that earned it.
items.wrong_way: Leaving pre-CTS uncertainty in the signoff scenario — the design closes against a phantom budget, paying area and power for margin that does not exist, or failing to close at all on paths that were never really late. Opposite error: relaxing everything at once post-CTS with no skew data, and discovering the truth at route signoff.
items.defense: A documented uncertainty schedule tied to named flow stages; each relaxation justified by the previous stage's skew report; the schedule reviewed like any other constraint artifact.
items.signoff_risk: Too tight: buffer bloat and possibly unclosable paths, plus erosion of trust ('just add uncertainty' culture). Too loose: late-stage timing surprises when real skew appears, at the point where the fix costs the most.
items.node_era_note: at 28nm pre-CTS uncertainty was tens of ps against a ~1GHz-class clock; at 7nm-and-below it is a larger fraction of a shorter period and is corner-specific, so a single schedule no longer suffices

items.pattern_name: Mode-scoped case analysis and per-mode exception scoping
items.situation: The chip has functional, scan-shift, scan-capture, bist, and low-power modes with constant pins; exceptions that are true in one mode are wrong in another.
items.derivation: 1) Build the mode table from the spec: each mode with its constant pins (test_se, scan_en, bist_run, power-mode straps). 2) Per mode scenario: set_case_analysis on the constants, then scope exceptions to that mode only — the exception file is generated from the table, not accumulated by hand over revisions. 3) Exclusivity rule: any claimed-false path must cite mode + constant value + why the endpoint is unreachable in that mode; a path false in functional mode but live in scan mode may NOT be false-pathed in the test scenario. 4) Regression guard: audit each mode's exceptions — any false path firing without an active case-analysis justification is an error, not noise.
items.wrong_way: A global false-path list inherited across all modes: a path structurally dead in functional mode but live in scan-shift escapes test-mode checking and fails at bring-up. The mirror error: missing case analysis forces the engine to time impossible paths, closure time explodes, and someone then adds false paths to cope — compounding the first error.
items.defense: The mode table reviewed jointly with DFT; per-mode exception diffs between releases; the automated audit proving every exception cites a mode.
items.signoff_risk: Too loose: silicon fails in the unscoped mode, typically scan or a power-mode entry, after full functional signoff looked clean. Too tight: closure drowned in impossible paths, and the pressure response (more false paths) converts a nuisance into the too-loose failure.

items.pattern_name: Asynchronous reset constraint: assertion async by construction, deassertion synchronized and bounded
items.situation: An asynchronous reset distributes to flops; assertion is intentionally asynchronous while deassertion must be synchronized, and the constraints must keep the recovery/removal checks alive.
items.derivation: 1) Treat assertion (async pin assert vs clock) as asynchronous by construction — the checks that matter are recovery (deassert) and removal (assert), which the tools apply to timed reset signals. 2) Synchronize deassertion: route the async reset through a reset synchronizer (two-flop) clocked by the destination domain. 3) Constrain the crossing INTO the reset synchronizer with bounded set_max_delay of order one destination period (confidence 0.4) rather than a blanket false path or a domain-wide clock group that swallows it — the bounded crossing preserves recovery/removal checks on the synchronizer flops; a domain-wide exception deletes them silently. 4) Bound reset distribution after the synchronizer (set_max_delay on the reset net, order of one destination period, confidence 0.4) so all flops exit reset within one cycle and removal skew stays inside a known window.
items.wrong_way: set_false_path from the reset source everywhere: recovery/removal checks vanish on the very flops that synchronize deassertion, metastable exit from reset passes signoff, and the chip fails as random bring-up crashes that look like software bugs.
items.defense: Reset-tree schematic; a report demonstrating recovery/removal checks present on the synchronizer flops; the removal-window arithmetic for the distribution bound.
items.signoff_risk: Too tight: aggressive distribution bounds create fake removal failures on large trees, tempting their removal. Too loose: no report flags the missing synchronizer checks — the escape is invisible until silicon, in the most intermittent failure class.

items.pattern_name: block-boundary I/O delay budget split
items.situation: Deriving set_input_delay / set_output_delay for a hierarchical block whose neighbors are not yet implemented or whose internal timing is still fluid
items.derivation: Start from the common period T of the interface clock. Reserve a fixed chip-level margin M (typically 10-20% of T). Split the remainder (T-M) into three parts: launch-block internal path budget L, interconnect/board/wire budget I, capture-block internal path budget C, with L+I+C = T-M. For an input delay the constraint becomes set_input_delay = L+I (or a chosen fraction); for output delay set_output_delay = C+I. Arithmetic shape: input_delay = (T-M)*f_launch_interconnect where f is usually 0.4-0.6 depending on which side owns more logic. Numbers assumed: M=15% of T (confidence 0.55), L:I:C split ≈ 40:20:40 (confidence 0.5)
items.wrong_way: Copying a flat full-chip I/O delay or using the entire period minus only clock uncertainty; this either starves the neighbor blocks of budget or leaves the current block with an unrealistically easy constraint that hides internal problems until integration
items.defense: Show the arithmetic split against the interface clock period, the reserved margin, and the relative logic depth expected on each side of the boundary; cite any existing similar interfaces already closed at those fractions
items.signoff_risk: Too tight: block fails timing even though the real system path would close, causing unnecessary ECOs or frequency reduction. Too loose: block closes easily but the integrated system fails at the boundary, forcing late redesign of both sides
items.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below higher relative variation and OCV usually force a larger reserved margin M than typical 28nm budgets

items.pattern_name: false-path versus multicycle-path decision
items.situation: A path exists in the netlist between two flops but is either functionally unreachable or is allowed more than one cycle by protocol
items.derivation: First prove functional unreachability (case analysis, formal, or exhaustive simulation of the enabling conditions). If unreachable under all legal modes → set_false_path. If reachable but the protocol guarantees N cycles of separation (e.g., a handshake that asserts only every Nth cycle) → set_multicycle_path -setup N -hold N-1 (or the appropriate hold adjustment). The multicycle value N is taken directly from the protocol specification or from the minimum observed separation in directed tests, never from a timing report
items.wrong_way: Declaring a false path simply because the path is not critical or because it is long; or setting multicycle without adjusting hold, which creates optimistic hold analysis and real silicon races
items.defense: Present the functional proof (waveform, state-machine excerpt, or formal property) that shows either unreachability or the guaranteed N-cycle separation; never defend solely with 'it timed'
items.signoff_risk: False path that is actually reachable: real timing violation in silicon, often intermittent. Multicycle too aggressive (N too large): same silicon failure. Multicycle too conservative or missing hold adjustment: either unnecessary timing pressure or hold violations that appear only after CTS

items.pattern_name: synchronous clock-domain-crossing constraint
items.situation: Two clocks are known to be synchronous (same source, defined phase relationship) and data crosses between them
items.derivation: Use create_generated_clock or set_clock_groups -asynchronous only if truly async. For synchronous crossings, leave the path timed but budget the available window as the phase difference minus setup/hold requirements of the capture flop minus any known skew bound. If the phase relationship is fixed by a PLL or divider, the constraint is simply the normal setup/hold check under the defined clocks; no extra exception is added unless an explicit multicycle or false-path justification exists
items.wrong_way: Blindly applying set_clock_groups -asynchronous to any crossing, which disables all timing checks and hides real violations when the clocks are actually synchronous
items.defense: Show the common root clock, the generation relationship (divider/PLL), and the static phase offset; demonstrate that the timed window is still positive after OCV
items.signoff_risk: Treating a synchronous crossing as async: silent functional failure when the phase relationship is violated by jitter or mis-lock. Over-constraining a true sync crossing: unnecessary timing ECOs on a path that already has adequate phase margin
items.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below larger on-chip variation makes the residual phase margin after OCV smaller, so engineers more often add explicit skew bounds

items.pattern_name: early over-constraint with planned relaxation
items.situation: During floorplan / placement / early CTS the design is intentionally given tighter constraints than the final target so that implementation produces extra margin
items.derivation: Choose a final target period T_final. For early stages use T_early = T_final * (1-k) where k is typically 0.05-0.15. Keep the same exceptions (false paths, multicycle) but scale only the clock period or the I/O delays. After CTS and before final routing, restore T_final and re-optimize. The value of k is chosen so that the extra margin roughly equals the expected degradation from CTS latency, routing detour and OCV increase
items.wrong_way: Leaving the over-constraint in place through signoff, or relaxing too early (before CTS) so that the recovered margin is immediately consumed by later stages
items.defense: Show the planned schedule of constraint tightening/relaxation points and the measured margin recovery at each stage; cite historical degradation numbers from similar blocks
items.signoff_risk: Never relaxing: final timing is artificially tight, causing needless area/power or frequency loss. Relaxing too early or too much: late-stage violations appear that could have been avoided by keeping pressure on the tools longer
items.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below higher late-stage degradation from routing and variation usually forces a larger early k than was common at 28nm

items.pattern_name: virtual clock for external I/O modeling
items.situation: Chip-level or block-level I/O must be timed against an external device whose clock is not present inside the design
items.derivation: create_clock -name VIRTUAL_IF -period T on a virtual object (or on a port that is later declared virtual). Then set_input_delay / set_output_delay relative to VIRTUAL_IF, using the external device's output-valid / input-setup numbers plus board uncertainty. The virtual clock is never used as a source for any on-chip generated clock; it exists only to anchor the external delays
items.wrong_way: Attaching the external delay numbers to an internal clock, which incorrectly applies on-chip OCV and latency to an off-chip path and can create optimistic or pessimistic checks depending on the latency values
items.defense: Show the external device datasheet timing, the board-trace uncertainty, and that the virtual clock has no network latency inside the design
items.signoff_risk: Too-tight external numbers: chip fails timing against a board that would actually work. Too-loose numbers: chip passes STA but fails in the real system when the external device is slower or the board is longer than assumed

items.pattern_name: generated / divided clock constraint
items.situation: A clock is produced by a divider, clock gate with enable, or PLL feedback inside the design
items.derivation: create_generated_clock -source <master> -divide_by N (or -edges / -edge_shift for non-integer or phase-shifted cases) on the divider output pin. The tool then automatically derives the period and waveform. For a clock gate used only as an enable, prefer set_clock_gating_check or a generated clock with -combinational if the intent is to model the gated clock as a real clock network. Always verify that the generated clock is not also constrained by a conflicting create_clock on the same pin
items.wrong_way: Creating a primary create_clock on the divider output with a manually computed period; this severs the phase relationship to the master and disables correct inter-clock timing and latency propagation
items.defense: Show the divider RTL or schematic, the exact edge relationship, and that report_clocks shows the generated clock correctly parented to the master
items.signoff_risk: Missing or wrong generated-clock definition: inter-clock paths are timed with incorrect period or phase, producing both false violations and missed real violations. Over-constraining with an extra create_clock: double-counting of latency and skew

items.pattern_name: asynchronous interface quasi-static constraint
items.situation: Data crosses between two truly asynchronous clocks (no known phase relationship) and the design uses synchronizers
items.derivation: set_clock_groups -asynchronous -group {clkA} -group {clkB} (or the equivalent set_false_path between the two clock domains). Then separately constrain the synchronizer chain: the first synchronizer flop is allowed to go metastable; the path from the first to the second synchronizer flop is timed for the full destination period (or a multicycle if the synchronizer is multi-stage and the protocol allows). No setup/hold check is required on the async arrival itself; the constraint only ensures the synchronizer resolves before the data is consumed
items.wrong_way: Leaving the async paths timed as ordinary synchronous paths (produces meaningless violations) or forgetting to time the synchronizer-to-logic paths, allowing the metastable value to be sampled by downstream logic
items.defense: Show the synchronizer structure, the MTBF calculation or stage count, and that set_clock_groups covers exactly the async domains without accidentally cutting synchronous paths
items.signoff_risk: Missing async exception: flood of false violations that hide real problems. Overly broad async exception that also cuts a synchronous path: real timing bug reaches silicon. Under-constraining the synchronizer output path: functional failure under rare phase alignments
items.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below higher metastability susceptibility sometimes forces an extra synchronizer stage compared with 28nm practice

items.pattern_name: pre-implementation inter-block budget handshake
items.situation: Two blocks that will later be integrated must each be given I/O constraints now, before either is fully implemented
items.derivation: Agree on a common interface clock period T. Allocate a shared interconnect budget I (wire, muxing, or feed-through). Remaining budget B = T - M - I is split by negotiation according to relative expected logic depth or by equal share if unknown. Block A receives output_delay = its share of B plus half of I; Block B receives the complementary input_delay. Both sides document the assumed numbers so that later integration can re-balance if one side closes with excess margin
items.wrong_way: Each block independently assumes it can consume most of the period, producing a pair of constraints that cannot be satisfied simultaneously when the blocks are stitched
items.defense: Present the written budget table signed by both owners, the reserved margin, and the plan for re-budgeting after first integration timing
items.signoff_risk: Budgets that sum to more than available period: integration fails and both blocks must be reopened. Budgets that are collectively too pessimistic: both blocks over-design, wasting area and power
