items.pattern_name: Block boundary I/O delay budget for unimplemented blocks
items.situation: Two blocks are being implemented in parallel and their top-level routing is not yet complete; input and output delays must be negotiated before physical integration.
items.derivation: 1. Start with clock period P. 2. Subtract clock uncertainty U (assumes 50 ps at 28nm, confidence 0.6) and setup margin M (assumes 10% of P, confidence 0.7) to get available budget B = P - U - M. 3. Estimate interconnect delay I from floorplan distance d and average intermediate-metal delay (assumes 120 ps/mm, confidence 0.6). 4. Negotiate split between launch and capture blocks based on RTL complexity; if complexity is equal, each gets (B - I)/2. 5. set_input_delay on the capture block = launch_budget + I = (B + I)/2. 6. set_output_delay on the launch block = capture_budget + I = (B + I)/2. 7. Document assumptions in the constraint header.
items.wrong_way: Split the period 50/50 without accounting for interconnect distance or relative logic depth. One block receives an impossible budget while the other has unusable slack, and top-level integration fails because the slack-rich block was optimized for area rather than speed.
items.defense: Show the floorplan distance, RTL complexity comparison such as pipeline depth or gate count, and reference actual achieved delays from a previous project on the same node.
items.signoff_risk: Too tight -> block fails timing and requires a late ECO or respin. Too loose -> block passes standalone but top-level integration fails because the external delay was underestimated, requiring late-stage top-level buffer insertion.
items.node_era_note: at 7nm and below, wire delay is less dominant but RC variation is higher, so margin increases and wire delay estimates are more uncertain

items.pattern_name: False path versus multicycle path from control-signal analysis
items.situation: A path in the netlist is not intended to be a single-cycle path, such as a register loaded by a decimated clock enable or a logically impossible combination.
items.derivation: 1. Trace the capturing flop's enable signal back to its source, which may be a counter, pulse generator, or gating logic equation. 2. Determine the minimum stable interval N in clock cycles from RTL inspection or simulation. 3. If the data source is guaranteed stable for N cycles and the capture only occurs on the Nth cycle, apply set_multicycle_path -setup N and set_multicycle_path -hold N-1. 4. If the path is logically never exercised for functional data transfer, such as a constant tie-off or scan-only path, apply set_false_path. 5. Verify with a waveform or formal property check before review.
items.wrong_way: Declare a false path when the path is actually a multicycle functional path. The tool ignores the path entirely, so if the enable logic has a bug and the path is exercised in a single cycle, silicon fails silently because no timing check ever existed.
items.defense: Show the RTL enable equation or a simulation waveform proving the N-cycle interval. For a false path, show the constant tie-off or mutually exclusive select logic that makes the path logically unreachable.
items.signoff_risk: Too loose (false path when multicycle needed) -> functional failure if the path is accidentally exercised single-cycle. Too tight (multicycle when false path sufficient) -> wasted optimization effort and possible congestion from unnecessary buffering.
items.node_era_note: at 7nm and below, complex clock gating and enable logic make multicycle derivation harder; at 28nm, simple counter-based enables were more common

items.pattern_name: Gray-code FIFO pointer CDC max_delay constraint
items.situation: A clock-domain crossing carries gray-coded FIFO pointers from one domain to another.
items.derivation: 1. Identify source and destination clocks and determine the faster period P_fast = min(P_src, P_dest). 2. Gray-code encoding guarantees only one bit changes per increment, but the entire bus must propagate within one receiving clock period to avoid sampling a multi-bit transition. 3. Apply set_max_delay -datapath_only from source to destination equal to P_fast (confidence 0.8), or 0.8 times P_fast for margin (confidence 0.6). 4. Do not apply set_false_path, because that would remove all timing checks and allow arbitrary delay. 5. Optionally add set_bus_skew if the tool supports it.
items.wrong_way: Set false path on the gray-code pointer bus. The tool ignores timing, so if a logic error causes two bits to toggle or if routing delay exceeds one clock period, the destination samples an invalid code and the FIFO corrupts data silently.
items.defense: Show the gray-code encoding table and explain that max_delay ensures the single-bit transition is captured within one cycle. Reference the CDC verification report or protocol specification.
items.signoff_risk: Too loose (false path) -> FIFO pointer mismatch, data loss, or system lock-up. Too tight (max_delay significantly less than P_fast) -> impossible routing, forced buffer chains, and power or area bloat.
items.node_era_note: at 7nm and below, on-chip variation makes max_delay harder to meet, so some teams use quasi-synchronous schemes or hard FIFO macros instead

items.pattern_name: Early-implementation over-constraining budget
items.situation: Pre-CTS synthesis and placement need margin for unknown clock skew, variation, and late ECOs.
items.derivation: 1. Estimate expected post-CTS skew S from a previous project on the same node (assumes 80 ps at 28nm, confidence 0.6). 2. Estimate OCV impact D as a percentage of nominal period (assumes 15%, confidence 0.6). 3. Reserve ECO margin E (assumes 5% of P_nominal, confidence 0.5). 4. Compute effective period P_eff = P_nominal - S - (D * P_nominal) - (E * P_nominal). 5. Apply P_eff during synthesis and initial placement. 6. After CTS, measure actual skew S_actual and relax toward P_nominal if the actual skew is smaller than estimated.
items.wrong_way: Over-constrain by a fixed large percentage such as 30% without a basis in estimated skew or variation. The tool inserts excessive buffers, causing congestion and power issues that are difficult to undo when relaxing later.
items.defense: Present a spreadsheet with the skew estimate, OCV table from library characterization, and historical ECO count from a previous project on the same node.
items.signoff_risk: Too tight -> excessive buffering, congestion, and power or area bloat that may not fully recover on relaxation. Too loose -> no headroom for CTS skew or late ECOs, causing a signoff crunch and potential silicon failure.
items.node_era_note: at 7nm and below, AOCV and POCV replace flat OCV derates, so over-constraining uses statistical margins rather than flat period subtraction

items.pattern_name: Virtual-clock-based IO delay from board and package parameters
items.situation: The chip interfaces with external devices and the board-level clock arrives at the pad, requiring constraints that account for off-chip delays.
items.derivation: 1. Create a virtual clock V with the same period and waveform as the board clock. 2. Estimate package trace delay T_pkg (assumes 100 ps for wirebond, confidence 0.6). 3. Estimate PCB trace delay T_pcb from trace length and dielectric constant (assumes 6-7 ps/mm, confidence 0.7). 4. For inputs, set_input_delay = T_ext_tco + T_pcb + T_pkg. 5. For outputs, set_output_delay = T_pcb + T_pkg + T_ext_setup. 6. Reference virtual clock V on all IO constraints so that internal clock insertion delay is not incorrectly applied.
items.wrong_way: Use the internal clock directly as the reference for set_input_delay without a virtual clock. The tool incorrectly accounts for internal clock latency, causing IO timing to be off by the insertion delay, which is on the order of 200-500 ps.
items.defense: Show the board stackup, package length extraction or IBIS model, and the external device datasheet specifying Tco and setup values.
items.signoff_risk: Too tight -> IO passes in block-level signoff but fails in system test. Too loose -> internal paths are over-optimized to compensate for the IO budget, wasting power and area.
items.node_era_note: at 7nm and below, high-speed SerDes and source-synchronous interfaces dominate, making virtual-clock-based SDC less common than protocol-specific timing models

items.pattern_name: RTL-complexity-based timing budget for unimplemented blocks
items.situation: Two blocks have not yet been synthesized and there is no gate-level netlist to measure actual path delays, but a boundary budget must be established.
items.derivation: 1. Estimate combinational depth for each block from RTL by counting logic levels between flops, for example Block A at 8 levels and Block B at 4 levels. 2. Apply historical delay per level L from the same node library (assumes 35 ps per level at 28nm typical VT, confidence 0.6). 3. Compute raw estimates D_A = levels_A * L and D_B = levels_B * L. 4. Add margin M for unknown optimization (assumes 25%, confidence 0.5). 5. Allocate budget proportionally: Block_A_budget = P * D_A / (D_A + D_B + I), where I is estimated interconnect delay. 6. Set input and output delays to match the negotiated budgets.
items.wrong_way: Split the clock period 50/50 regardless of logic depth or complexity. The deep block receives an impossible budget and requires late restructuring, while the shallow block finishes quickly with slack that cannot be transferred across the boundary.
items.defense: Show the RTL levelization report and reference previous block actuals demonstrating the correlation between level count and achieved delay on the same node.
items.signoff_risk: Too tight -> deep block fails timing and requires pipeline insertion or architecture change. Too loose -> shallow block is optimized for area rather than speed, and top-level integration fails because its output delay was underestimated.
items.node_era_note: at 7nm and below, delay per level varies widely with VT and track type, making raw level count less predictive

items.pattern_name: Clock gating setup and hold check derivation
items.situation: An integrated clock gating cell must be constrained so that the enable signal does not change near the active clock edge and create a glitch.
items.derivation: 1. Extract the ICG library setup T_setup_lib and hold T_hold_lib from the timing library, for example 40 ps setup and 30 ps hold (confidence 0.8). 2. Estimate clock skew U between the enable launch flop and the ICG cell based on the clock tree plan (assumes 50 ps, confidence 0.6). 3. Derive effective setup = T_setup_lib + U and effective hold = T_hold_lib + U, conservatively adding the skew magnitude regardless of direction. 4. Apply set_clock_gating_check -setup [effective_setup] -hold [effective_hold]. 5. Verify against the post-CTS skew report in the gating region.
items.wrong_way: Use the raw library setup and hold values without adding skew uncertainty. If the enable launch flop and the ICG are physically separated, clock skew can cause the enable to arrive after the clock edge, producing a glitch on the gated clock.
items.defense: Show the CTS skew estimate for the gating region and the library characterization values for the specific ICG cell.
items.signoff_risk: Too loose -> clock glitches, functional failure, and sporadic silicon bugs. Too tight -> impossible to meet with realistic skew, causing the tool to insert unnecessary buffers on the enable path.
items.node_era_note: at 7nm and below, clock mesh and multi-source CTS reduce ICG skew sensitivity, but glitch windows are narrower due to higher frequency

items.pattern_name: Combinational feedthrough max_delay budgeting
items.situation: A hard macro or block contains a pure combinational path from an input pad to an output pad that must meet a system-level delay requirement.
items.derivation: 1. Determine the system-level requirement T_system from the top-level timing budget, for example 2 ns. 2. Subtract input pad delay T_inpad and output pad delay T_outpad from the library (assumes 100 ps each, confidence 0.7). 3. Compute remaining budget B = T_system - T_inpad - T_outpad. 4. Apply set_max_delay -datapath_only -from [input] -to [output] B. 5. Do not use set_false_path because the path must meet board-level timing.
items.wrong_way: Leave the path unconstrained or apply set_false_path. If no clock is present the path is unchecked; if a virtual clock is present the tool may apply an arbitrary period. The path fails at board-level timing test.
items.defense: Show the board-level timing budget and the pad delay extraction from the library, demonstrating that the macro budget is a derived subset of the system requirement.
items.signoff_risk: Too loose -> system-level setup failure at board test. Too tight -> impossible macro timing that requires pipeline insertion or a specification change.
items.node_era_note: at 7nm and below, pure combinational feedthroughs are rare due to high integration; at 28nm they were common in IO macros

items.pattern_name: Post-CTS clock uncertainty update from actual skew
items.situation: After clock tree synthesis, the pre-CTS pessimistic uncertainty must be replaced with realistic numbers for signoff.
items.derivation: 1. Run CTS and extract actual global skew S_global and local skew S_local from the CTS report. 2. Add PLL jitter J from the device datasheet. 3. Add margin M for residual on-chip variation (assumes 5% of period for setup, confidence 0.6). 4. Compute setup uncertainty = S_global + J + M. 5. Compute hold uncertainty = S_local + J + M_hold. 6. Replace the pre-CTS pessimistic uncertainty with these computed values. 7. Re-run static timing analysis.
items.wrong_way: Keep the pre-CTS uncertainty, which was intentionally pessimistic to account for unknown skew. After CTS this double-counts the actual skew and causes over-design in the final stages.
items.defense: Show the CTS skew report and the PLL jitter specification, and explain that the margin is a percentage of period based on historical variation from the same node.
items.signoff_risk: Too tight -> area and power bloat from over-pessimism that cannot be recovered late in the flow. Too loose -> setup or hold failures at signoff if actual variation exceeds the reduced budget.
items.node_era_note: at 7nm and below, POCV and statistical timing reduce the need for flat uncertainty margins, though skew and jitter remain

items.pattern_name: Mode-based case analysis for multiplexed clocks
items.situation: A block has multiple clocks selected by a multiplexer, such as a functional clock and a slower test clock.
items.derivation: 1. Identify the select signal for the clock mux, for example TEST_EN. 2. Apply set_case_analysis 0 or 1 to the select pin to disable the inactive clock tree during each mode. 3. Derive constraints for functional mode with the functional clock period P_func. 4. Derive constraints for test mode with the test clock period P_test, which is often slower, for example by a factor of 10. 5. Run separate timing sessions or use multi-mode analysis. 6. Verify that no paths are timed between mutually exclusive clocks.
items.wrong_way: Constrain both clocks simultaneously without case analysis. The tool analyzes cross-domain paths between functional and test flops, reporting massive false violations and causing over-design or impossible closure.
items.defense: Show the mux RTL and the test protocol document specifying the clock frequencies and mode selection per test phase.
items.signoff_risk: Too loose (no case analysis and modes switch dynamically) -> missing real paths in untested mode combinations. Too tight (both modes active) -> false violations, wasted engineering time, and over-optimization.
items.node_era_note: at 7nm and below, UPF-based power intent and multi-mode multi-corner analysis formalize mode handling; at 28nm, manual set_case_analysis was more common

items.pattern_name: Block-boundary input/output delay budgeting between unimplemented blocks
items.situation: Top-level integration where Block A launches to Block B and neither block is implemented yet, need to assign set_input_delay to B and set_output_delay from A to close top level early
items.derivation: Step1: Get top-level period T (e.g., T=1000ps confidence 1.0 if given). Step2: Estimate top-level interconnect between blocks: assumes 15% of T for 28nm (confidence 0.6) and 25% of T for 7nm-and-below (confidence 0.55) due to via resistance. So T_interconnect = T * 0.15 (confidence 0.6). Step3: Estimate uncertainty/jitter: assumes 10% of T (confidence 0.65) for setup. Step4: Remaining budget T_remain = T - T_interconnect - T_uncert = T * 0.75 (confidence 0.6). Step5: Split between launch and capture based on logic depth from RTL: if balanced, 50%/50% of T_remain (confidence 0.6); if one block is known control-heavy, 40%/60% (confidence 0.5). Step6: For Block B input: set_input_delay -max = T_launch + T_interconnect (e.g., 0.375*T + 0.15*T = 0.525*T). For Block B input -min for hold: assumes 10% of T (confidence 0.5) to ensure short path not over-optimistic. For Block A output: set_output_delay -max = T_capture + T_interconnect.
items.wrong_way: Assign 50% period to each block and 0% to interconnect, or assign set_input_delay = 0.5*T and set_output_delay = 0.5*T independently, double-counting period and leaving no room for top-level wire; downstream fails with uncloseable top-level paths after both blocks harden, requiring ECO re-budget
items.defense: Show RTL stage count estimate per block, historical wire delay from previous similar floorplan with similar bump pitch, and top-level floorplan distance estimate; keep budget spreadsheet with T_launch/T_interconnect/T_capture columns and review with both block owners; validate with zero-interconnect top-level trial route
items.signoff_risk: Too tight (over-budgeting interconnect/launch): block becomes bloated, inserts excess buffers, area/power spiral, may still pass signoff but fails PPA; Too loose (under-budgeting interconnect): block passes alone but top-level fails setup with real wires, requires late re-budget and full block re-implementation
items.node_era_note: At 28nm interconnect estimate 10-15% of period was safe; at 7nm-and-below need 20-30% plus via ladder and BEOL variation margin due to thin wires

items.pattern_name: False path vs multicycle path decision and defense
items.situation: Long timing path that looks like setup failure but is functionally not exercised every cycle, e.g., config register to datapath, mode mux, one-hot FSM branch, or debug path
items.derivation: Step1: Trace enable condition: does path go through a MUX select that is static for N cycles? Check RTL: if select comes from config reg that only writes on boot, N >= 10 cycles (confidence 0.7). Step2: Check temporal exclusivity: can launch and capture happen in same cycle per spec? Run formal reachability or check simulation that config write and datapath active are mutually exclusive. Step3: If mutually exclusive never in same cycle for functional operation, candidate for set_false_path. If mutually exclusive for K cycles but re-converges, candidate for set_multicycle_path K. Example: N=2 cycles for double-flop mode change (confidence 0.6), so set_multicycle_path -setup 2 -hold 1. Step4: Validate that all side-paths covered: ensure no other timing arc uses same net without the static condition. Step5: Require waiver: list startpoint-endpoint pair plus RTL condition signal name.
items.wrong_way: Mark any failing long path as false path to close timing quickly without proving static condition, or mark a true multicycle as false, or mark as multicycle 2 when hold needs explicit -hold 1 handling; silently breaks because synthesis/place no longer fixes path, but in rare functional mode path is active and silicon fails at speed or hold fails in silicon due to missing hold multicycle
items.defense: Provide waveform showing config stable for >N cycles, formal proof of mutual exclusivity, or static signal tied in this mode (case analysis); show CDC or mode constraint file that forces MUX select; get architect sign-off on mode table; keep false path list in version-controlled exceptions file with comment referencing spec section
items.signoff_risk: Too loose (false when should be multicycle or timed): path unbounded, late transition causes functional failure at speed, not caught at signoff STA because exception hides it; Too tight (timed when should be false): over-constrains implementation, creates congestion and setup/hold ping-pong, may still signoff but with PPA penalty and possible hold fixes that hurt setup
items.node_era_note: At 28nm false paths often tolerated; at 7nm-and-below false paths hide OCV and aging effects, reviewers require formal proof plus set_clock_groups handling

items.pattern_name: Clock-domain crossing max-delay budgeting for 2-flop sync and async FIFO
items.situation: Signal crossing from clkA to clkB asynchronous, protected by 2-flop synchronizer or async FIFO pointers, need SDC to prevent STA from timing it as synchronous
items.derivation: Step1: Identify sync chain: first flop after crossing is synchronizer, mark set_false_path or set_asynchronous_group between clocks, or set_max_delay -datapath_only. Step2: For data with valid handshake, constrain data delay to be less than destination period to ensure it is stable when sampled: assumes max allowed = 80% of min(dest period, source period) (confidence 0.6) minus 15% margin for jitter (confidence 0.55). Example: if dest period = 1000ps (confidence 1.0), set_max_delay = 800ps (confidence 0.6) -datapath_only from launch to first sync flop. Step3: For FIFO pointers gray-coded, set_max_delay = 1 * dest period (confidence 0.65) and set_min_delay = 0 for hold. Step4: Do NOT cut control path with same max: sync chain itself gets set_false_path -from launch -to sync0 to allow unlimited metastability resolution time, but keep set_max_delay on data bus.
items.wrong_way: Apply set_clock_groups -asynchronous to both data and control without max-delay, which allows data to have infinite delay and FIFO pointer to drift multiple cycles, causing functional CDC bug that STA hides; or apply set_false_path to data bus instead of control, silently allowing 10ns route on 1GHz interface
items.defense: Show synchronizer schematic, point to 2-flop chain in RTL, provide CDC tool report (e.g., Questa CDC) that data is qualified by synchronized valid, and show max-delay report that data arrives within one dest clock; retain pointer gray-coding proof
items.signoff_risk: Too loose (pure false path on data): CDC passes STA but fails in silicon due to data changing during sync window, metastability + data incoherence, signoff CDC checker will flag unbounded delay; Too tight (max-delay too small, e.g., 20% of period): implementation over-constrains, fails to route, forces unnecessary pipelining
items.node_era_note: At 28nm set_clock_groups -asynchronous often sufficient; at 7nm-and-below need set_max_delay -datapath_only plus OCV-aware margin due to larger variation on short cross-domain nets

items.pattern_name: Early over-constraining and staged relaxation
items.situation: Early floorplan/placement stage where wire estimates are optimistic and late degradation from CTS, routing, and OCV is expected
items.derivation: Step1: Start with target period T. Step2: Apply over-constraint factor: assumes 15% over-constraint (confidence 0.6) at synthesis, so T_synth = T * 0.85 (confidence 0.6). Step3: Add clock uncertainty: assumes 10% of T for early stage (confidence 0.65) vs 5% at signoff (confidence 0.7). Step4: Keep input/output delays at nominal, do NOT over-constrain both period and IO simultaneously; only over-constrain core. Step5: Staged relaxation: after CTS, relax to 7% over-constraint (confidence 0.55) (T * 0.93), after route to 3% (confidence 0.5) (T * 0.97), before signoff to 0%. Step6: Track slack histogram: if worst slack >20% of T (confidence 0.6) early, indicates too much margin still available.
items.wrong_way: Over-constrain period by 30% (confidence misapplied) AND set_input_delay to 60% of period AND set_output_delay to 60% of period simultaneously, creating impossible 120% budget that forces tool to bloat logic and insert buffers everywhere, leading to power/area blowup and later unfixable congestion
items.defense: Show historical degradation curve from previous similar design: synthesis to place ~5% loss (confidence 0.55), place to CTS ~5% (confidence 0.55), CTS to route ~5-8% (confidence 0.5); justify over-constraint factor as sum of expected degradation; track QOR trend weekly and relax only when slack stable for 2 runs
items.signoff_risk: Too tight early: implementation becomes unnecessarily large, high power, congestion prevents closure, may still signoff but with 20-30% area penalty; Too loose early: early optimism hides real failures, late surprise with -200ps slack at route requiring full re-synthesis
items.node_era_note: At 28nm 10% over-constraint often enough; at 7nm-and-below need 15-20% due to via resistance and low-Vdd variation, but must relax earlier to avoid excessive low-Vt usage

items.pattern_name: Virtual clock for IO budgeting
items.situation: Chip-level IO interface where external device clock does not exist inside chip, need to model external launch/capture for set_input_delay and set_output_delay
items.derivation: Step1: create_clock -name VCLK -period T_ext equal to external device period (e.g., T_ext=1000ps confidence 1.0). Step2: Set virtual clock latency = 0 (confidence 1.0) because no internal network, but set uncertainty = board jitter + chip jitter: assumes 10% of T_ext (confidence 0.6). Step3: For input: set_input_delay -clock VCLK -max = T_board_max + T_ext_Tco_max + margin. Example: board delay max 300ps (confidence 0.6), Tco max 400ps (confidence 0.6), margin 50ps (confidence 0.5), so input max = 750ps. Set -min = board min + Tco min - margin (e.g., 100ps + 100ps -50ps =150ps). Step4: For output: set_output_delay -clock VCLK -max = T_board_max + T_setup_external (e.g., 300ps+200ps=500ps confidence 0.6), -min = T_board_min - T_hold_external.
items.wrong_way: Constrain IO using internal generated clock that includes internal insertion delay, causing double-counting of clock latency: input delay appears to have extra 500ps insertion, tool over-constrains data path and fails IO timing that is actually external-only; or using same clock for both input and output with zero virtual latency causing hold miscalculation
items.defense: Provide external device datasheet Tco/Tsu/Th numbers, board trace length to delay conversion (approx 6ps per mm (confidence 0.5)), and show virtual clock has no source latency; cross-check with IBIS or board simulation; keep VCLK separate per IO bank
items.signoff_risk: Too tight (large input/output delay): chip fails to close IO timing, adds unnecessary pipeline, may still signoff but with reduced Fmax; Too loose (small delay): chip passes internal STA but fails at system level on board, setup/hold failure at external device not caught until lab
items.node_era_note: At 28nm virtual clock latency 0 was sufficient; at 7nm-and-below need to model board and package via separate clock latency and include package trace variation

items.pattern_name: Generated and divided clock constraint derivation
items.situation: Internal clock divider, muxed clock, or PLL output that is not master clock, need correct timing relationship for STA
items.derivation: Step1: Master clock period T_master (e.g., 1000ps confidence 1.0). Step2: create_generated_clock -source [get_pin divider/Q] -divide_by N (e.g., N=2 confidence 1.0) so T_gen = T_master * N = 2000ps. Step3: If divided by 2 with 50% duty, set edges -edges {1 3 5} or -divide_by 2. Step4: Clock latency: generated clock latency = master insertion + divider cell delay: assumes divider delay 30ps (confidence 0.5) + wire 20ps (confidence 0.5). Step5: Uncertainty: master uncertainty 50ps (confidence 0.6) + divider jitter 20ps (confidence 0.5) = 70ps total (confidence 0.55). Step6: Set clock groups: if muxed clocks are mutually exclusive, set_clock_groups -physically_exclusive, else -logically_exclusive; do NOT use -asynchronous unless truly asynchronous.
items.wrong_way: Create generated clock with -combinational instead of -divide_by, losing edge relationship and causing STA to analyze 1-cycle path as 2-cycle or vice versa; or forget to set generated clock source latency, leading to 0 skew assumption and hold failures in silicon; or use set_clock_groups -asynchronous for muxed synchronous clocks, hiding synchronous transfer
items.defense: Show clock divider schematic, simulation showing divided edge aligns to master, and report_clocks showing master is source; verify with report_clock -skew that generated relationship matches RTL expectation; check that generated clock period matches measured division in gate sim
items.signoff_risk: Too tight (wrong divide factor, e.g., divide_by 4 instead of 2): half the paths appear as multicycle incorrectly, tool under-fixes, silicon fails at double frequency; Too loose (false -asynchronous between related generated clocks): cross-clock paths not timed, potential setup/hold failure between divide domains that are actually synchronous
items.node_era_note: At 28nm generated clock auto-derived often worked; at 7nm-and-below need explicit -master_clock and latency adjustment due to large divider variation and duty-cycle distortion

items.pattern_name: System-synchronous and source-synchronous output budgeting with board trace
items.situation: Chip drives data and clock/strobe to external device, need to split timing budget between chip, board, and external setup/hold
items.derivation: Step1: External device requires T_setup_ext = 200ps (confidence 0.6) and T_hold_ext = 100ps (confidence 0.6) at its pins. Step2: Board trace mismatch between clock and data: assumes max skew 50ps (confidence 0.55) due to 8mm mismatch (6ps/mm confidence 0.5). Step3: For source-synchronous (clock and data both from chip, edge-aligned): set_output_delay -max = T_board_max + T_setup_ext + board_skew_max = 300ps+200ps+50ps=550ps (confidence 0.6), set_output_delay -min = T_board_min - T_hold_ext - board_skew (e.g., 100ps-100ps-50ps = -50ps) meaning hold may be negative allowed. Step4: For system-synchronous (common board clock): output delay must include full period: set_output_delay -max = T_period - (T_setup_ext + board). Step5: Add margin 5% of period (confidence 0.6) for OCV.
items.wrong_way: Use same output delay for both source-sync and system-sync, ignoring that source-sync budget is board+setup only while system-sync includes period, causing either impossible timing (system-sync too tight) or under-constrained source-sync that fails on board due to unmodeled trace skew
items.defense: Provide board stackup and trace length report, external device datasheet with setup/hold numbers, and diagram showing clock-data alignment (center-aligned vs edge-aligned); show calculation spreadsheet with board min/max separate and justify margin from SI simulation
items.signoff_risk: Too tight: over-constrains output path, forces large drivers and hurts power, may still signoff but with SI issues; Too loose: chip passes STA but board fails because external setup/hold violated in corner, found only in lab with pattern-dependent failures
items.node_era_note: At 28nm board skew 50ps often negligible vs 2ns period; at 7nm-and-below with 1GHz+ source-sync, 50ps board skew is 5% of period and must be budgeted explicitly

items.pattern_name: Asynchronous handshake interface max/min delay constraint
items.situation: Asynchronous SRAM, flash, or custom handshake where request, address, data have no common clock, timing is relative between signals
items.derivation: Step1: Identify handshake: e.g., req launches, ack returns, data must be stable before ack. Step2: Do NOT use set_input_delay with period; use set_max_delay and set_min_delay between related signals. Step3: Example: req to data valid: set_max_delay -from [get_ports req] -to [get_ports data] = T_external_access_max + board_max = 10ns (confidence 0.6) (e.g., SRAM access 8ns (confidence 0.6) + board 2ns (confidence 0.5)). Step4: Hold: set_min_delay = board_min + hold requirement of external device = 1ns (confidence 0.5). Step5: For bidirectional, separate read and write constraints with -rise/-fall and case analysis on direction pin. Step6: False path all unrelated clocks to these IOs to avoid period-based analysis interfering.
items.wrong_way: Constrain async interface with create_clock + set_input_delay using arbitrary 10ns period, causing STA to check against non-existent clock edge and either miss true max-delay violation or create artificial multicycle; or apply set_false_path to entire async interface, allowing unbounded delay and silicon read failure
items.defense: Provide external device timing diagram showing req->data relationship without clock, and board trace delays; show that max-delay constraint directly models access time, not period; include protocol assertion that req de-asserts after ack, proven by formal
items.signoff_risk: Too tight (max-delay too small): implementation fails to meet impossible async timing, forces unnecessary pipelining and area; Too loose (false path): path can be 20ns but STA reports no violation, chip fails to read external memory at speed, caught only in system test
items.node_era_note: At 28nm async interfaces often handled with simple false path; at 7nm-and-below need explicit max/min delay plus SI-aware derating due to long board traces and on-die variation

items.pattern_name: Block-Boundary Output/Input Delay Budget Split
items.situation: Two blocks (A and B) share a clock and are being implemented independently. Block A feeds data to Block B through top-level routing. Each block needs its own SDC with boundary delay constraints.
items.derivation: 1. Combinational-path budget = T_period - T_setup - T_clock_uncertainty.  Example at 500 MHz: 2000ps - 50ps (confidence 0.5) - 120ps (confidence 0.6) = 1830ps.  2. Estimate interconnect delay from floorplan: T_inter ≈ 300-500ps for a moderate top-level route (confidence 0.5).  3. Split remaining time by estimated block complexity: T_A_budget / T_B_budget proportional to each block's combinational-depth × gate-delay estimate.  4. set_output_delay on A = T_inter + T_B_budget.  5. set_input_delay on B = T_A_budget + T_inter.  6. Verify self-consistency: A's available = budget - output_delay = T_A_budget; B's available = budget - input_delay = T_B_budget.
items.wrong_way: (a) set_output_delay = T_inter only, ignoring capture-block share → A is under-constrained internally and B is over-constrained by the amount of B's budget that A silently consumed.  (b) 50/50 split regardless of complexity → one block starved, the other has excessive slack.  (c) Forgetting clock_uncertainty → budget is 100-200ps optimistic, and the error accumulates silently through integration.
items.defense: Present the floorplan-derived interconnect estimate, each block's gate-equivalent count or combinational depth, and the resulting slack distribution. If one block's initial implementation shows very negative or very positive slack, adjust the split and re-budget.
items.signoff_risk: Too-tight output delay on A: Block A over-designed (area/power bloat) and may still fail, blocking integration. Too-loose output delay on A: A finishes easily but the interconnect + B path overflows the period at integration, requiring either interconnect buffering (area + power) or A re-implementation (schedule risk).
items.node_era_note: At 7nm, interconnect RC is much higher so the interconnect share of the budget grows from roughly 20-25% to 30-40% (confidence 0.6), changing the typical split ratio.

items.pattern_name: False Path vs Multicycle Path Decision for Inter-Clock Paths
items.situation: Two clock domains exist in the design. The engineer must decide whether paths between them should be set_false_path, set_multicycle_path, or constrained as single-cycle.
items.derivation: 1. Determine if clocks share a common root (same PLL or oscillator).  2. If NO common root → clocks are asynchronous → false-path the data paths, but constrain synchronizer paths separately (see Synchronizer Max-Delay pattern).  3. If common root with different frequencies → compute LCM period: LCM(T_A, T_B). MCP_setup = LCM / T_capture.  4. Always set MCP_hold = MCP_setup - 1 to move the hold check to the correct launch-capture edge pair.  5. If same frequency with known phase offset → model with set_clock_latency -source and constrain as single-cycle with the offset accounted for.
items.wrong_way: (a) set_false_path on a path whose clocks share a root → real timing violation ignored, silicon failure.  (b) set_multicycle_path N -setup without also setting set_multicycle_path (N-1) -hold → tool performs hold check on wrong edge: either generates false hold violations (area waste from unnecessary buffers) or misses real hold violations.  (c) Blanket set_false_path between two domains to 'clean up reports' → masks paths that should be timed, including paths through combinational logic between domains that bypass the synchronizer.
items.defense: Show the clock-generation schematic (PLL → divider → clock tree) proving the relationship. Present the LCM edge diagram with launch and capture edges marked. Demonstrate the hold-edge adjustment is correct by showing the actual waveform.
items.signoff_risk: False path too aggressive: real path untimed, functional silicon failure. False path too conservative (should be false but isn't): wasted optimization cycles and area, but functionally safe. Multicycle without hold adjustment: false hold violations waste area, or real hold violations on the wrong edge escape to silicon.
items.node_era_note: no-era-difference-recalled — the logical decision tree is the same regardless of process node.

items.pattern_name: set_max_delay on Synchronizer Clock-Domain Crossing
items.situation: A signal crosses from clock domain A to domain B through a 2-FF synchronizer. The path to the first synchronizer flop needs a real timing constraint, not a false-path.
items.derivation: 1. The path from the source register in domain A to the D pin of the FIRST synchronizer flop in domain B IS timed.  2. set_max_delay on this path = T_capture_period (ensures data arrives within one capture cycle without demanding single-cycle tightness).  3. set_false_path -hold on this same path (hold timing is meaningless through a synchronizer because metastability makes the capture-edge relationship non-deterministic).  4. Paths through the second synchronizer flop onward: set_false_path (data is now synchronized).  5. Identify each synchronizer instance explicitly by cell name or by hierarchical path — do not rely on clock-domain crossing auto-detection.
items.wrong_way: (a) set_false_path on the entire crossing including the path to the first flop → path can be arbitrarily long, widening the metastability window and degrading MTBF.  (b) Apply normal set_max_delay without setting -hold false_path → tool inserts hold buffers on the synchronizer path, adding latency that may exceed the max_delay target or defeat the purpose.  (c) set_max_delay globally to all paths between the two domains instead of targeting the synchronizer flop → over-constrains data paths that should be false-path'd.
items.defense: List each synchronizer instance by hierarchical name. Show the set_max_delay value justified as one capture-clock period. Reference the MTBF requirement (from reliability spec) that justifies the synchronizer depth. Show that hold-false-path is applied to prevent buffer insertion.
items.signoff_risk: Too-tight max_delay: unnecessary optimization on synchronizer paths, area waste, possible routing congestion near synchronizer cells. Too-loose max_delay: data arrives late, first flop samples transitioning data, MTBF degrades or functional failure. Missing hold false-path: tool inserts delay buffers that increase latency on the synchronizer path, partially defeating the max_delay constraint.
items.node_era_note: At 7nm, faster clock frequencies mean the absolute max_delay value is smaller, making the path-to-synchronizer constraint tighter and increasing the chance that even a modest-length route violates it.

items.pattern_name: Over-Constraining at Synthesis with Gradual Relaxation Toward Signoff
items.situation: Starting implementation of a new block. Target clock period is known, but the design will degrade during CTS (insertion delay), routing (parasitics), and signoff (OCV, IR-drop). The constraint must leave room for this degradation.
items.derivation: 1. At synthesis: target period × (1 - early_margin). Typical early_margin = 25-30% (confidence 0.6). At 500 MHz (2ns): synthesize to ~1.4-1.5ns.  2. After placement: relax to period × (1 - mid_margin). Typical mid_margin = 10-15% (confidence 0.5). Target ~1.7-1.8ns.  3. After CTS: relax to period × (1 - late_margin). Typical late_margin = 3-5% (confidence 0.6).  4. At signoff: use full period with all parasitics, OCV, IR-drop annotated.  5. The margin values are calibrated from prior tapeouts at the same node on the same team's designs.
items.wrong_way: (a) Synthesize to 100% of period from the start → after CTS and routing add 200-400ps of degradation, design is significantly negative → many ECO iterations, schedule risk.  (b) Synthesize to 50% of period → massive over-design: area 20-40% larger than necessary (confidence 0.5), power significantly higher, and the tool optimizes paths that don't need it.  (c) Relax constraints too aggressively between stages (e.g., jump from 70% to 100% after placement) → catch timing problems too late when they're expensive to fix.
items.defense: Present the empirical degradation curve from the team's prior designs at the same node: average insertion-delay as % of period, average routing-parasitic impact, typical OCV impact. Show the margin schedule matches this historical data.
items.signoff_risk: Over-constrained at synthesis: area and power waste but functionally safe — expensive chip, meets schedule. Under-constrained at synthesis: area-efficient but timing closure becomes a multi-iteration nightmare at signoff — tapeout delay risk, possible missed market window.
items.node_era_note: At 7nm, OCV derates and IR-drop effects are larger, so the early margin typically needs to be 35-40% versus 25-30% at 28nm (confidence 0.6). The relaxation schedule has more stages.

items.pattern_name: Async FIFO Gray-Code Pointer Synchronization Constraints
items.situation: An asynchronous FIFO bridges two clock domains. Gray-code pointers cross from write domain to read domain (and vice versa) through synchronizer chains. The constraint must protect data integrity while bounding pointer propagation delay.
items.derivation: 1. Data path through FIFO: set_false_path from write-clock domain to read-clock domain on data bits (FIFO depth protects data — no timing constraint needed).  2. Gray-code pointer bits from write side to read side: set_max_delay = T_read_period per bit (ensures each pointer update arrives within one read-clock cycle).  3. Similarly for read-to-write pointer: set_max_delay = T_write_period.  4. set_false_path -hold on all pointer synchronizer paths (hold timing meaningless through synchronizers).  5. Each pointer bit gets an independent set_max_delay to ensure all bits of the same pointer arrive within the same capture window.
items.wrong_way: (a) set_false_path on everything including pointer bits → pointer propagation is unconstrained, may take many cycles, FIFO full/empty detection becomes unreliable, data corruption through read-before-write-complete or write-before-read-complete.  (b) set_max_delay on pointer bits to a value much larger than the capture period → pointer update delayed by multiple cycles, requiring deeper FIFO than implemented, functional overflow/underflow.  (c) Using set_multicycle_path on pointer bits instead of set_max_delay → meaningless for truly asynchronous clocks with no fixed phase relationship.
items.defense: Show the FIFO depth analysis: depth must be greater than 2 × (max_delay / period) for safe full/empty detection. List each pointer bit's max_delay constraint. Reference synchronizer MTBF analysis for the chosen synchronizer depth. Show waveform diagram of pointer update timing.
items.signoff_risk: Unconstrained pointer (false path): subtle data corruption when write side overwrites data before read side consumes it — extremely hard to reproduce in simulation, manifests as rare data errors in silicon. Over-constrained pointer (max_delay too tight): area waste from buffer insertion on pointer paths, possible routing congestion near synchronizers, but functionally safe.
items.node_era_note: At 7nm, faster clock frequencies mean the absolute max_delay is smaller and FIFO depth requirements are proportionally larger for the same synchronization latency budget.

items.pattern_name: Generated/Divided Clock Constraint Derivation
items.situation: A flip-flop or latch divides the master clock by N, producing a slower clock that drives downstream logic. The SDC must correctly define the generated clock and its relationship to the master.
items.derivation: 1. Define master clock first: create_clock -name mclk -period T [get_ports mclk_pin].  2. Define generated clock: create_generated_clock -name gclk -source [get_pins div_reg/CK] -divide_by N [get_pins div_reg/Q].  3. Generated period = N × T.  4. Source pin MUST be the clock-input pin of the divider register (CK), not the data-output pin (Q). The tool traces from source to output automatically.  5. Set clock uncertainty on the generated clock domain: includes master PLL jitter + divider-edge jitter + guard band.  6. For paths between master and generated domains: compute edge relationships and determine if multicycle constraints are needed (fast-to-slow may need MCP; slow-to-fast is typically single-cycle).
items.wrong_way: (a) create_clock on the divider output with a manually specified period instead of create_generated_clock → the tool does not know the master-generated relationship, cannot compute inter-domain timing, latency and insertion delay are wrong.  (b) Specify -source as div_reg/Q (output pin) instead of div_reg/CK (clock pin) → tool fails to trace through the divider correctly, latency calculation wrong by the divider's clock-to-Q delay.  (c) Forgetting clock uncertainty on the generated clock → zero jitter assumed, timing too optimistic by the jitter amount.  (d) Not handling the edge relationship between master and generated clocks → hold violations on fast-to-slow crossings that are invisible in single-edge analysis.
items.defense: Show the clock-generation RTL or schematic. Present the waveform diagram with master and generated edges aligned. Prove the edge relationship (which master edge corresponds to which generated edge). Demonstrate that uncertainty is set for both domains.
items.signoff_risk: Wrong generated period: all downstream timing wrong — paths either over-constrained (area waste) or under-constrained (silicon failure). Missing inter-domain constraints: paths between master and generated clock untimed, functional failure. Wrong source pin: latency off by the divider's clk-to-Q delay, setup/hold margins incorrect.
items.node_era_note: no-era-difference-recalled — the SDC construct is identical; at 7nm jitter is proportionally larger relative to the period, making the uncertainty setup more critical but not changing the pattern.

items.pattern_name: Virtual Clock and IO Delay Budgeting for External Interfaces
items.situation: Chip IO ports interface with external components (memory, PHY, other chips). The internal clock tree does not reach the IO, and the external timing reference may differ from the internal clock.
items.derivation: 1. Create a virtual clock matching the external reference: create_clock -name virt_clk -period T_ext (no physical pin, or on a reference clock input).  2. For input ports: set_input_delay -clock virt_clk -max D_in [get_ports data_in].  D_in = T_ext_clk2q (from external chip datasheet) + T_board_trace (from PCB extraction) + T_margin.  3. For output ports: set_output_delay -clock virt_clk -max D_out [get_ports data_out].  D_out = T_board_trace + T_ext_setup (from external chip datasheet) + T_margin.  4. T_margin = 10-15% of T_ext (confidence 0.6).  5. T_board_trace = from PCB team's post-layout extraction or pre-layout estimate: typically 0.5-3ns depending on board (confidence 0.5).  6. Internal clock defined separately on the actual clock input pin of the chip.
items.wrong_way: (a) set_input_delay relative to the internal clock instead of the virtual clock → tool includes internal clock-tree latency in the IO timing calculation. The external device does not see the internal clock tree, so this is wrong by the clock-tree latency amount.  (b) Forgetting the board trace delay → timing optimistic by 0.5-3ns, silicon works in the lab but fails on the actual board with real trace lengths.  (c) Using the internal clock period when it differs from the external period → constraining to the wrong frequency, either over- or under-constraining IO paths.
items.defense: Present the external chip datasheet with highlighted timing parameters (clk-to-output, setup time). Show the PCB team's trace-delay extraction report. Display the resulting IO timing budget with the margin clearly separated. Show a timing diagram with external and internal clock edges.
items.signoff_risk: Input delay too tight: internal paths to IO registers over-designed, area/power waste. Input delay too loose: data arrives at IO register too late, IO interface fails on actual board. Output delay too tight: output path over-designed. Output delay too loose: data arrives at external receiver too late, external device fails to capture.
items.node_era_note: At lower nodes with multi-GHz SerDes IO, the trace delay is a much larger fraction of the period and jitter is more significant, making the IO budget much tighter and the margin more critical (confidence 0.7).

items.pattern_name: Clock Uncertainty Budget Decomposition
items.situation: Setting set_clock_uncertainty for a clock domain. The value must aggregate multiple real-world sources of timing variation, and the correct value changes as the design progresses through the flow.
items.derivation: 1. Total uncertainty = T_jitter + T_skew + T_guard.  2. T_jitter (PLL output jitter): from PLL datasheet or PLL team characterization. Typically 2-5% of period (confidence 0.6). At 500 MHz: 2ns × 3% ≈ 60ps.  3. T_skew (clock tree skew): before CTS, use an estimate based on design size — typically 50-150ps (confidence 0.5). After CTS, use the actual reported skew from CTS timing reports.  4. T_guard (margin): 5-15% of (jitter + skew) (confidence 0.5).  5. Apply at each flow stage: (a) Pre-CTS synthesis/implementation: set_clock_uncertainty = jitter + skew_estimate + guard. (b) Post-CTS: set_clock_uncertainty = jitter + guard (remove skew_estimate since actual skew is now known). (c) Inter-clock crossings: add additional inter-clock uncertainty on top (typically larger, covering both PLLs' jitter).
items.wrong_way: (a) Single flat uncertainty value for the entire flow → too optimistic before CTS (skew unknown), too pessimistic after CTS (estimated skew still in the number).  (b) Forgetting to reduce uncertainty after CTS → design over-constrained by the estimated-skew amount, unnecessary buffering and area waste.  (c) Using PLL jitter alone without skew → underestimate by 50-150ps, silicon fails under clock-tree skew conditions especially at worst-case PVT corners.  (d) Same uncertainty for intra-domain and inter-domain paths → inter-domain uncertainty should be larger because it covers jitter from two independent PLLs.
items.defense: Show the PLL jitter specification (datasheet excerpt). Show the CTS skew report (or estimation methodology if pre-CTS). Present a table of uncertainty values at each flow stage. Demonstrate that inter-clock uncertainty is appropriately larger than intra-clock.
items.signoff_risk: Uncertainty too large: over-designed clock tree, extra buffers and area, power waste — functionally safe but expensive. Uncertainty too small: timing violations under real jitter + skew conditions, functional failure at high temperature or low voltage corners — these failures are often intermittent and hard to diagnose.
items.node_era_note: At 7nm, PLL jitter is a larger fraction of the period (faster clocks, similar absolute jitter), and OCV derates effectively increase the skew component, so total uncertainty is a much larger fraction of the period than at 28nm (confidence 0.7).

items.pattern_name: block-input delay (forward budget)
items.situation: Block A is being implemented independently; its inputs arrive from upstream logic whose timing is not yet finalized. The block-level SDC must carry an input delay constraint that is achievable but not so loose that the block passes internally while the full chip fails.
items.derivation: Step 1: establish the reference clock period P (e.g., 1 ns at 1 GHz). Step 2: subtract a margin factor M (typical practice: reserve 10–20% of period for inter-block uncertainty; confidence on 15% as typical mid-range: 0.6). Result: available input budget = P × (1 − M). Step 3: the block internally must meet its own setup time Tsu before the capture edge; so input delay constraint = P × (1 − M) − Tsu. In practice this is written as: set_input_delay $clock [minus_M * P] −clock_fall −add_delay. The −clock_fall flag appears because the capture edge is often on the falling edge for source-synchronous or half-cycle budgets.
items.wrong_way: Setting input delay to a fixed arbitrary value (e.g., 0.5 ns) without relation to the clock period — this creates a constraint that may be unachievable at slow corners or so loose at fast corners that the block passes internally but fails at top-level; it also prevents the synthesis tool from knowing how hard to optimize the input paths.
items.defense: In review the engineer shows that the input delay equals the clock period minus the downstream block's setup requirement minus the inter-block interconnect estimate — a three-line arithmetic trace; additionally, the constraint is verified against the top-level timing report after integration to confirm the budget was correct.
items.signoff_risk: Too tight: the block's synthesis will over-optimize paths that should be allowed to use the full clock period, wasting area and power on gates that will be irrelevant once the full chip is integrated. Too loose: the block will pass internally but the top-level timing closure will fail because the upstream logic cannot actually achieve the budget; ECO insertion at top level is expensive.
items.node_era_note: At 7nm and below, the interconnect delay estimate used in Step 2 must include an on-chip variation (OCV) adjustment that is larger than at 28nm; also, the derate factor for interconnect delay across corners is often set more conservatively (confidence on 20% OCV adjustment as typical at 7nm: 0.5) because within-die variation is more significant.

items.pattern_name: block-output delay (backward budget)
items.situation: Block A must drive its outputs to downstream Block B; Block B has not been implemented yet. The output delay constraint on Block A's outputs must be derived from what Block B can reasonably accept, not from what Block A can theoretically produce.
items.derivation: Step 1: reference clock period P. Step 2: subtract Block B's internal clock-to-Q delay Tcq (from the target library; if unknown, use an upper-bound estimate from a similar library, confidence on using 200–400 ps as a starting estimate for Tcq: 0.65). Step 3: subtract Block B's setup time Tsu. Step 4: subtract inter-block interconnect delay estimate Dinter (if unknown, use a conservative initial estimate; confidence on Dinter being treated as negligible at early project stages: 0.5). Result: set_output_delay constraint = P − Tcq − Tsu − Dinter. The constraint is written on Block A's output ports, referencing the same clock that Block B will use.
items.wrong_way: Setting output delay to zero or to the full clock period — zero implies the output must arrive at the same time as the clock edge (achievable only for source-synchronous interfaces), while full-period setting wastes the entire budget and may cause the synthesis tool to under-optimize the output paths.
items.defense: Engineer shows the arithmetic: the output delay represents the time available from Block A's launch clock edge to when Block B must capture, broken into Block B's Tcq + Tsu + interconnect; the trace is updated once Block B's library data is available.
items.signoff_risk: Too tight: Block A's output paths are over-constrained; synthesis may add unnecessary buffering or fail to meet timing, creating a block-level timing failure that will disappear once the full chip integrates. Too loose: Block B will receive data with excessive uncertainty, requiring Block B to have larger setup margins that consume chip-level timing margin.

items.pattern_name: false path exception and its defense
items.situation: A set of paths is logically impossible to exercise in functional operation (e.g., paths through a configuration register that can only be written during test mode, or paths between two clock domains that are never simultaneously active), but STA will analyze them and fail timing on them.
items.derivation: Step 1: identify the functional condition under which the path can be exercised; if the condition is logically impossible (configuration is read-only during functional operation, the two clocks are never on simultaneously), the path is a true false path. Step 2: define the false path with sufficient precision: the constraint must identify the specific clock pair, the specific start and end points, and the condition — e.g., set_false_path −from [get_clocks clk_a] −to [get_clocks clk_b] −through [get_pins block/config_reg_reg/Q]. Step 3: confirm no other path between those endpoints exists that could exercise the same data relationship through a different route.
items.wrong_way: Setting a broad false path on an entire clock domain or a large group of registers without specifying the exact paths — this silently hides real timing failures because the tool stops analyzing all paths between those domains even ones that ARE exercisable; the review will pass because the constraint is correct in spirit but the implementation is too broad.
items.defense: Engineer presents the functional specification (register documentation, clocking diagram, or FSM state table) showing the specific condition that makes the path impossible; the false path constraint is written to match that specific condition, and the review checks that no other functional path exists between the same endpoints.
items.signoff_risk: Too tight (false path is incorrect — the path IS exercisable functionally): the path is never optimized and never fixed, causing a silent timing failure that will appear on silicon. Too loose (false path is correct but written too narrowly): the false path constraint does not cover the actual failure path and the violation remains; the engineer will spend time trying to fix a path that should have been excepted.
items.node_era_note: At 7nm and below, false paths that rely on clock domain never being simultaneously active must also be reviewed against clock gating synthesis — the synthesis tool may combine clock enables in ways that create momentary simultaneous switching that the original false path analysis did not anticipate; confidence on this specific risk: 0.55.

items.pattern_name: multicycle path — launch/capture edge offset
items.situation: A data path is known to take more than one clock cycle to produce a valid result (e.g., a hardware accelerator that produces a result after 3 clock cycles, or a datapath with deliberate pipelining). The synthesis tool must be told not to optimize the path as a single-cycle path.
items.derivation: Step 1: determine the number of cycles N from launch to when data is valid at the capture register. Step 2: for a setup (max-delay) path, write set_multicycle_path N −setup −from [launch_reg] −to [capture_reg] − this moves the capture edge from the nominal edge to edge N. Step 3: for a hold (min-delay) path, write set_multicycle_path N−1 −hold −from [launch_reg] −to [capture_reg] − this prevents the hold check from being placed at the new capture edge (which would be too aggressive). The arithmetic: capture edge for setup = launch edge + N periods; capture edge for hold = setup capture edge − 1 period.
items.wrong_way: Setting only the setup multicycle path without the hold multicycle path — this moves the setup capture edge to N but leaves the hold check at the new edge, which is N−1 periods from launch, making the hold constraint artificially aggressive by one cycle and causing hold violations on paths that are actually valid.
items.defense: In review, the engineer presents the FSM state diagram or pipeline description that defines the exact number of cycles the data is valid after launch; the multicycle path constraint is written with both −setup and −hold statements, and the arithmetic (setup edge = N, hold edge = N−1) is explicitly shown.
items.signoff_risk: Too tight (N is smaller than actual): synthesis attempts to meet a single-cycle timing on a path that physically requires more cycles, resulting in either over-area or a setup violation that will never close. Too loose (N is larger than actual): the path is given more time than it needs, reducing optimization priority on paths that should be optimized, and potentially masking real single-cycle paths that happen to share some logic.
