items.pattern_name: CDC path — synthesizable safety budget
items.situation: Two clock domains are asynchronous to each other (no fixed phase relationship) and data crosses between them. The CDC path must be constrained to prevent STA from analyzing it as a synchronous path, but also must carry a clock uncertainty budget for the metastability resolution margin.
items.derivation: Step 1: set_false_path between the two clock domains (logical exception: there is no single capture edge to analyze against). Step 2: add a clock uncertainty budget representing the worst-case clock skew plus the metastability resolution time required for the synchronizer flip-flop to settle — in practice this is derived as: uncertainty = clock_skew_estimate + Tmetastability_estimate. Typical clock skew estimate for a given clock domain pair: 100–300 ps depending on clock tree depth (confidence on 200 ps as a starting estimate for moderate-depth trees: 0.6). Typical metastability resolution time: 200–500 ps for a two-flop synchronizer in a standard library (confidence on 300 ps for a typical 28nm library: 0.55). Total uncertainty budget: 500 ps. This is applied as set_clock_uncertainty on the path or as a latency budget on the receiving domain.
items.wrong_way: Setting only the false path without any clock uncertainty budget on the receiving domain — this means the CDC path is completely unanalyzed and any timing failure in the synchronizer logic (which is real and can cause data corruption) will not appear in STA; alternatively, applying a very large clock uncertainty that covers the entire clock period essentially excepts the paths without any analysis, masking real functional failures.
items.defense: Engineer presents the clock tree depth reports for both domains, the estimated skew between them, and the synchronizer cell's metastability specification from the library databook; the uncertainty value is the arithmetic sum of skew and metastability budget.
items.signoff_risk: Too tight (uncertainty budget is smaller than actual skew + metastability): the CDC path will appear to meet timing in STA but will have real metastability failures on silicon; this is a silent data corruption failure. Too loose: the receiving domain will be over-constrained relative to its actual clock quality, causing unnecessary timing failures in the CDC receiver logic.
items.node_era_note: At 7nm and below, the metastability resolution time for standard-cell synchronizers increases because the smaller transistor sizes have lower drive strength for the same geometry, and the difference between best-case and worst-case metastability resolution widens; confidence on this: 0.55; as a result, CDC uncertainty budgets at 7nm often use a larger metastability margin (500 ps instead of 300 ps).

items.pattern_name: inter-block timing budget split
items.situation: Two blocks (Block X and Block Y) are being implemented in parallel by different engineers; they share a top-level timing budget of P nanoseconds for paths between them. The budget must be split between Block X's output paths, the interconnect, and Block Y's input paths before either block is implemented.
items.derivation: Step 1: establish total budget B = P − top_level_setup_margin (confidence on using 5–10% of period as top-level margin: 0.65). Step 2: allocate to Block X output paths: Bx = B × α where α is the area/power budget fraction agreed between block owners (or equally: 0.5). Step 3: allocate to Block Y input paths: By = B × β where β = 1 − α minus interconnect share. Step 4: interconnect delay share Dinter = B − Bx − By (typically small for on-chip connections, large for package-level connections). In practice: set_output_delay [Bx] −clock [clk] −from [BlockX/outputs] and set_input_delay [By] −clock [clk] −to [BlockY/inputs].
items.wrong_way: Both engineers independently assume the other block will absorb the timing margin and constrain their block at full clock period — this double-counts the budget and the top-level integration will fail with no room left; or, one engineer constrains at full period and the other at near-zero, creating an unbalanced design.
items.defense: The lead timing engineer presents the top-level timing budget spreadsheet showing the arithmetic split, agreed in writing between block owners before implementation begins; at block reviews the constraints are compared against this agreement.
items.signoff_risk: Too tight for either block: that block's implementation will fail timing internally even if the other block's implementation succeeds, requiring ECO and potentially redesign. Too loose for either block: that block will consume more timing margin than allocated, leaving insufficient margin at top level for interconnect and clock skew, causing a top-level timing failure.
items.node_era_note: At 7nm and below, interconnect delay estimates for on-chip paths are less predictable due to increased coupling capacitance sensitivity to routing geometry; confidence on needing a larger interconnect delay estimate margin at 7nm (20% vs. 10% at 28nm): 0.55.

items.pattern_name: over-constraining during early implementation
items.situation: A block is being implemented early in the project timeline before the full chip clock frequency is finalized. The engineer wants to constrain the block conservatively so that if the clock frequency increases later, the block does not need to be re-timed.
items.derivation: Step 1: take the target clock period P_target and apply an over-constraint factor F (confidence on F = 0.85 to 0.90 being common practice: 0.65 — meaning constrain to 85–90% of the target period). Step 2: write the clock constraint as create_clock −period [P_target × F]. Step 3: document the relaxation point: when the full chip frequency is confirmed, the constraint will be relaxed to full period. The over-constraint is typically applied in the initial synthesis run; place-and-route may use a less aggressive over-constraint.
items.wrong_way: Over-constraining without a documented relaxation plan — the block passes timing at the over-constrained frequency but the constraint is never relaxed, so the block is under-utilized (over-area, over-power) compared to what it would be at the actual chip frequency; or, over-constraining by too much (e.g., F = 0.5) causing the block to fail timing even though the target frequency is achievable.
items.defense: Engineer presents the frequency plan showing the confirmed vs. targeted clock frequency, the over-constraint factor, and the explicit plan to relax to full period once frequency is confirmed; this is captured in the block's constraint documentation.
items.signoff_risk: Too tight (over-constraint is too aggressive, F too small): the block fails timing at the over-constrained frequency even though it would meet the actual target frequency; this is a false failure that wastes ECO cycles. Too loose (over-constraint is too mild, or not applied): if the chip frequency increases, the block must be re-timed, causing project schedule risk.
items.node_era_note: At 7nm and below, over-constraining is less common because the frequency targets are typically already finalized before implementation begins due to the long turnaround time at advanced nodes; confidence on this shift: 0.55.

items.pattern_name: virtual clock for IO timing
items.situation: A chip has IO signals that are timed relative to an external clock that is not inside the chip (e.g., DDR interface, source-synchronous input). The chip-level SDC must constrain the input and output paths relative to this external clock, which does not appear as a create_clock in the design.
items.derivation: Step 1: define the external clock frequency and characteristics as a virtual clock: create_clock −name virtual_sys_clk −period [P] (the virtual clock exists only as a reference for IO constraints, not as a physical clock inside the design). Step 2: for inputs: set_input_delay −clock virtual_sys_clk −clock_fall [Tdata_valid_max] [input_ports] where Tdata_valid_max is the maximum time after the external clock edge that the input data is valid (from the IO specification or board-level timing). Step 3: for outputs: set_output_delay −clock virtual_sys_clk −clock_fall [Tdata_setup_required] [output_ports] where Tdata_setup_required is the minimum time before the external clock edge that the output data must be stable. Step 4: verify that the input and output delay together leave at least a small positive margin for on-chip variation: P − input_delay − output_delay > 0.
items.wrong_way: Writing IO constraints without a virtual clock and referencing an internal clock instead — this creates a mismatch between the analysis viewpoint (chip-internal launch edge) and the actual IO timing (external clock domain), causing the input delay to be referenced from the wrong edge and producing incorrect timing analysis for the IO paths.
items.defense: Engineer presents the board-level timing diagram showing the external clock, the data valid window, and the setup/hold requirements; the virtual clock period and the input/output delay values are derived directly from that diagram and cross-checked against the board-level timing budget.
items.signoff_risk: Too tight: input or output delays are set shorter than the actual data valid window, causing the chip to fail IO timing in the system even though the internal timing is correct; this results in board-level failures that require chip respin or I/O driver changes. Too loose: input or output delays are set longer than the actual data valid window, masking real internal timing failures that will appear on the board; the chip passes silicon test but fails system-level test.
items.node_era_note: At 7nm and below, DDR and high-speed source-synchronous interfaces often require a derived clock (DCD-corrected or duty-cycle-corrected) for the virtual clock reference; the virtual clock period must account for the duty cycle distortion of the PLL, which adds an additional uncertainty term; confidence on this: 0.55.

items.pattern_name: generated (divided) clock constraint
items.situation: A clock divider or clock gate inside the design produces a divided clock that feeds registers in a specific block. The divided clock must be constrained as a generated clock so that timing is analyzed correctly relative to its parent clock.
items.derivation: Step 1: identify the clock divider or clock gate cell and the output pin of that cell that produces the divided clock. Step 2: define the generated clock: create_generated_clock −name [clk_div] −source [master_clock_pin] −div [N] [divider_output_pin] where N is the division factor (2 for divide-by-2, 4 for divide-by-4, etc.). Step 3: the tool automatically derives the period of the generated clock as N times the master clock period. Step 4: verify the phase relationship — a simple divider typically produces a divided clock that is edge-aligned with the master clock; if there is a phase offset (e.g., from a clock gate with an enable), add −phase [offset_degrees] to the generated clock definition. Step 5: check whether paths between the master clock domain and the divided clock domain are CDC paths (asynchronous) or synchronous (if the divider is glitch-free and the phase relationship is deterministic).
items.wrong_way: Defining the divided clock as a second independent create_clock instead of a create_generated_clock — this tells STA that the divided clock has its own unrelated period, breaking timing analysis for any path that crosses between the master and divided clock domains; paths that should be analyzed as single-cycle paths will be analyzed as asynchronous paths, or vice versa.
items.defense: Engineer presents the clock tree schematic showing the divider cell and its division factor, the phase relationship from simulation or timing simulation, and the generated clock SDC statement; the review checks that the division factor and source pin are correct and that the CDC classification between master and divided domain is documented.
items.signoff_risk: Too tight (dividing by a smaller factor than actual): the generated clock period is set too short, causing false setup violations on paths that are analyzed as faster than they actually are. Too loose (dividing by a larger factor than actual): the generated clock period is set too long, reducing optimization priority for paths on that clock and potentially masking real failures; also, paths crossing between master and divided domains will be incorrectly analyzed for CDC.
items.node_era_note: At 7nm and below, clock dividers are often implemented using clock gating cells rather than explicit divider circuits, and the division factor may be dynamically changed during operation; in these cases the generated clock must be constrained as a set of multiple generated clocks or with a −master_clock and −divide_by specification that accounts for all possible division modes; confidence on needing this multi-mode approach: 0.55.

items.pattern_name: asynchronous reset path constraint
items.situation: A design has an asynchronous reset signal (reset_n) that is not synchronous to any chip clock. Paths that originate from registers driven by the asynchronous reset must be constrained to prevent STA from analyzing them against an undefined clock relationship, while ensuring the reset path itself is safe (synchronous to the clock for release timing).
items.derivation: Step 1: identify the asynchronous reset source pin on registers that have async reset — e.g., preset/clear pins. Step 2: define a false path exception on the asynchronous reset signal: set_false_path −from [async_reset_port] −to [async_reset_receiver_pins] −this prevents STA from analyzing the reset signal's arrival time relative to the clock because the reset is not synchronous. Step 3: separately constrain the reset removal (deassertion) timing: the reset must be released and meet the recovery/removal time of the receiving register relative to the clock edge — this is written as set_max_delay [Trecovery] −from [async_reset_port] −to [register_async_pin] with a specific value derived from the library recovery time. Step 4: in practice, a two-stage synchronizer on the reset signal (for async reset) and a clock domain crossing constraint from the reset to each clock domain is added to ensure reset release is not synchronous to any functional clock edge.
items.wrong_way: Setting only a false path on the reset and not constraining the reset removal timing — the false path prevents setup analysis but the reset can still violate the recovery time of the receiving register, causing metastability or incorrect reset behavior when the reset is released near an active clock edge; alternatively, not synchronizing the reset at all and letting it directly drive async preset/clear pins of registers in multiple clock domains.
items.defense: Engineer presents the reset architecture diagram showing whether the reset is asynchronous-assert (immediate, no clock needed) and synchronous-deassert (must meet recovery time), the synchronizer chain for reset release, and the set_false_path and recovery-time constraints for each clock domain; the recovery time value is taken from the library databook.
items.signoff_risk: Too tight: recovery time constraint is set too small, causing false failures at slow corners where the actual recovery time is larger; or, false path is set too broadly, hiding real timing failures on paths that do interact with the reset in a clocked way (e.g., reset-gated logic). Too loose: recovery time constraint is set too large, wasting timing margin; or, false path is not applied and the reset path fails STA, causing unnecessary fixing of a path that should be excepted.
items.node_era_note: At 7nm and below, the recovery time of registers increases relative to the clock period at advanced nodes due to larger setup/recovery time in finFET cells; also, the powerup state requirements at 7nm often mandate a more complex reset architecture with retention registers that require separate timing constraints for the save/restore signals; confidence on increased recovery time as a significant factor at 7nm: 0.55.

items.pattern_name: block_boundary_io_delay_budgeting
items.situation: Deriving input/output delay budgets between two blocks with unknown internal timing, during top-level integration
items.derivation: Split the available clock period (T_clock) minus clock skew (T_skew, assumes 10% of T_clock confidence 0.7) and margin (T_margin, assumes 15% of T_clock confidence 0.6) between the launch block (T_launch), interconnect (T_interconnect), and capture block (T_capture) proportionally to their expected logic depth. Formula: T_launch + T_interconnect + T_capture ≤ T_clock - T_skew - T_margin. Allocate based on historical logic depth ratios from similar blocks.
items.wrong_way: Assuming an equal 33/33/33 split between launch, interconnect, and capture without considering block complexity, leading to one block being over-constrained while another has excessive slack
items.defense: Present historical data from similar blocks showing typical logic depth distributions and justify the proportional split based on gate count and pipeline depth
items.signoff_risk: Too tight: impossible timing closure for one block; Too loose: timing failures at integration when interconnect delay exceeds budget
items.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below: interconnect delay variability increases, requiring larger margins in T_interconnect

items.pattern_name: false_path_vs_multicycle_decision
items.situation: Determining whether a path that cannot meet single-cycle timing should be constrained as a false path or a multicycle path
items.derivation: Analyze the path's logical feasibility: if the path is structurally impossible (e.g., mutually exclusive enables, reset conditions), mark as false path. If the path is functionally valid but requires multiple cycles (e.g., multi-stage data transfer), mark as multicycle path with appropriate -setup and -hold values. For multicycle N: effective period = N * T_clock.
items.wrong_way: Marking a false path as multicycle (wastes cycles and may hide real timing issues), or marking a multicycle path as false (causes functional failure due to missing data latching)
items.defense: Review RTL code for logical impossibility (e.g., gated clocks, enable conditions) or multi-cycle requirements (e.g., pipeline stages, handshake protocols). Use formal verification to confirm.
items.signoff_risk: False path mislabeled as multicycle: unnecessary timing relaxation may hide real issues; Multicycle mislabeled as false: functional failure due to missing data capture
items.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below: more complex clock gating increases false path opportunities but also risk of mislabeling

items.pattern_name: clock_domain_crossing_cdc_constraint
items.situation: Constraining data transfer between asynchronous clock domains to prevent metastability
items.derivation: Insert synchronizer flops (typically 2-3 stages) in the receiving domain. Constrain the path from launch flop to first synchronizer flop as false or multicycle. Calculate setup/hold requirements based on clock frequencies: T_su = T_clock_receiver - T_skew - T_synchronizer_delay (assumes T_skew is 5% of T_clock confidence 0.8). Use set_clock_groups -asynchronous for the two domains.
items.wrong_way: Not constraining CDC paths at all, or using insufficient synchronizer stages (e.g., only 1 stage), leading to metastability propagation
items.defense: Reference CDC design guidelines and synchronizer verification reports. Show that synchronizer depth matches the required MTBF (mean time between failures) for the design.
items.signoff_risk: Too loose: metastability propagates to functional logic causing system failure; Too tight: impossible to implement due to excessive synchronizer delay
items.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below: higher clock frequencies require more synchronizer stages for same MTBF

items.pattern_name: early_implementation_overconstraining
items.situation: Setting initial timing constraints during early implementation when block timing is unknown
items.derivation: Start with tight constraints: set clock period to 80% of target (confidence 0.7), add 20% margin (confidence 0.6) on all paths. Gradually relax constraints as implementation matures, using actual timing data from block-level runs.
items.wrong_way: Starting with final relaxed constraints, missing early timing issues that could have been caught with tighter constraints
items.defense: Demonstrate iterative constraint relaxation: show progression (e.g., Week 1: 0.8*T, Week 2: 0.85*T, Week 3: 0.9*T) with corresponding implementation data.
items.signoff_risk: Too tight: unnecessary optimization effort and potential over-design; Too loose: late-stage timing failures when blocks cannot meet relaxed constraints
items.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below: more aggressive initial constraints needed due to higher process variability

items.pattern_name: virtual_clocks_for_io_interfaces
items.situation: Constraining IO interfaces where the actual clock is external and not part of the design
items.derivation: Create a virtual clock with the same period as the external IO clock. Use set_clock_groups -asynchronous for asynchronous IOs. Derive input delay as: T_input_delay = T_external_clock_period * 0.5 - T_setup_external (assumes T_external_clock_period confidence 0.9, T_setup_external confidence 0.7). Derive output delay as: T_output_delay = T_clock - T_hold_external - T_skew (assumes T_skew confidence 0.8).
items.wrong_way: Using the actual internal clock for IO timing instead of a virtual clock, causing incorrect timing checks at the IO boundary
items.defense: Reference IO timing specifications from the external system and show that virtual clock period matches the external clock specification.
items.signoff_risk: Wrong virtual clock period: IO timing failures at system integration; Incorrect delay calculation: setup/hold violations at IO boundaries
items.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below: IO timing margins tighter due to higher operating frequencies

items.pattern_name: generated_divided_clock_constraint
items.situation: Constraining a clock that is derived from another clock (e.g., divided, gated, or multiplied)
items.derivation: Use create_generated_clock -source [master_clock_pin] -divide_by N -name derived_clock. Add clock uncertainty: T_uncertainty = T_jitter_master + T_jitter_derived + margin (assumes T_jitter_master confidence 0.8, T_jitter_derived confidence 0.7, margin 10% of derived period confidence 0.6). Set clock latency based on divider logic delay.
items.wrong_way: Treating the derived clock as an independent primary clock, ignoring its relationship to the master clock, leading to incorrect timing analysis
items.defense: Show the clock tree structure and the divider logic. Reference the clock generation RTL and synthesis reports to confirm the division ratio and latency.
items.signoff_risk: Incorrect division ratio: wrong timing analysis for all paths using this clock; Missing uncertainty: setup/hold failures due to unaccounted jitter
items.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below: clock dividers more commonly implemented as part of clock network, requiring tighter uncertainty modeling

items.pattern_name: asynchronous_interface_constraint
items.situation: Constraining an interface between two blocks with no clock relationship (asynchronous)
items.derivation: Use set_clock_groups -asynchronous -group {clock1} -group {clock2}. For data transfer, insert handshake logic (e.g., request/acknowledge) and constrain the paths as false or multicycle. For synchronizers: use N-stage synchronizers with MTBF calculation: MTBF = (T_clock * 2^N) / (2 * T_metastability * T_frequency) (assumes T_metastability confidence 0.7).
items.wrong_way: Not using asynchronous clock groups, causing the timer to check paths between the domains and report false violations or miss real metastability issues
items.defense: Reference interface specification documenting the asynchronous nature. Show handshake RTL and synchronizer design that ensures safe data transfer.
items.signoff_risk: Missing asynchronous group: false timing errors and wasted optimization effort; Incorrect synchronizer constraints: metastability in functional logic
items.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below: higher operating frequencies require more robust handshake and synchronizer designs

items.pattern_name: inter_block_timing_budgeting_pre_implementation
items.situation: Allocating timing budgets between two blocks that have not been implemented yet, during architecture phase
items.derivation: Calculate available time: T_available = T_clock - T_skew (assumes 10% of T_clock confidence 0.7) - T_margin (assumes 20% of T_clock confidence 0.6). Allocate to blocks based on complexity: T_block1 = T_available * (complexity_block1 / total_complexity), where complexity is estimated from gate count and logic depth (assumes complexity estimation confidence 0.7).
items.wrong_way: Allocating equal timing budgets to both blocks regardless of their complexity, leading to one block being impossible to implement while the other has excessive slack
items.defense: Present block complexity estimates based on architectural specifications and historical data from similar designs. Justify the proportional allocation with expected gate counts and pipeline depths.
items.signoff_risk: Too tight for complex block: impossible timing closure; Too loose for simple block: wasted power and area due to over-optimization
items.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below: more accurate early complexity estimates possible due to better synthesis correlation

items.pattern_name: clock_latency_budgeting
items.situation: Accounting for clock network delay when deriving path timing constraints
items.derivation: Measure clock latency (T_latency) from clock tree synthesis. Derive available time for data path: T_data = T_clock - T_latency - T_skew (assumes T_skew confidence 0.8) - T_margin (assumes 10% of T_clock confidence 0.7). Allocate T_data to combinational logic based on path criticality.
items.wrong_way: Ignoring clock latency in timing budget, or double-counting it by including it in both clock and data path constraints, leading to incorrect timing analysis
items.defense: Reference clock tree synthesis reports showing actual latency values. Show that clock latency is only subtracted once from the clock period in the timing budget.
items.signoff_risk: Underestimated latency: setup violations due to insufficient time for data path; Overestimated latency: unnecessary pessimism leading to over-constrained design
items.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below: clock network latency more predictable due to better modeling, but more sensitive to process variations

items.pattern_name: uncertainty_allocation_in_derived_clocks
items.situation: Allocating clock uncertainty budgets for clocks with jitter and margin requirements
items.derivation: For a derived clock: T_uncertainty = T_jitter_source + T_jitter_derived + T_margin (assumes T_jitter_source confidence 0.8, T_jitter_derived confidence 0.7, T_margin 15% of clock period confidence 0.6). Subtract T_uncertainty from available time: T_available = T_clock - T_uncertainty - T_skew. Allocate remaining to data path.
items.wrong_way: Using the same uncertainty value for all clocks regardless of their source and derivation, leading to either over- or under-constrained paths
items.defense: Reference clock source specifications (e.g., PLL jitter specs) and jitter measurements from silicon data. Show that uncertainty values are specific to each clock domain.
items.signoff_risk: Too little uncertainty: timing failures due to unaccounted jitter; Too much uncertainty: over-constrained design with unnecessary power/area overhead
items.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below: clock jitter more significant due to higher frequencies, requiring more precise uncertainty modeling

items.pattern_name: Block-boundary input/output delay budget
items.situation: A block has synchronous inputs/outputs to an external device or another block, and the SDC must say how much delay lives outside the block boundary.
items.derivation: 1. Identify interface period P and capture clock relationship. 2. For an input, set_input_delay -max = external driver tco_max + interconnect_max + clock-offset_max + margin M; set_input_delay -min = external driver tco_min + interconnect_min + clock-offset_min - hold guard H. M is often 5% of P in early specs (confidence 0.4); H is often 0 unless min external delay is uncertain (confidence 0.5). 3. Verify feasibility: input_delay_max + worst internal input-to-flop delay + setup + clock uncertainty <= P. 4. For an output, set_output_delay -max = interconnect_max + downstream receiver input delay_max + clock-offset_max + M; the internal launch-to-port budget is then P - receiver_setup - output_delay_max - clock uncertainty. 5. For hold, check output_delay_min + min internal launch-to-port delay >= receiver hold.
items.wrong_way: Picking input/output delay as an arbitrary fraction of the period, or zero, without external timing data. This silently moves the impossible delay into the neighboring block or hides it entirely, so the block may pass standalone but fail at system integration.
items.defense: External device datasheet tco/setup/hold values, board trace length or package delay estimate, clock relationship diagram, and a margin register showing the negotiated M.
items.signoff_risk: Too tight: the block fails internally on unrealistic port budgets and wastes area/power fixing paths that are not the system problem. Too loose: the block signoff is clean but the interface fails on board or at integration.
items.node_era_note: at 7nm-and-below, clock uncertainty and derate consume a larger fraction of the period, leaving less room for arbitrary IO margin than at 28nm

items.pattern_name: False path versus multicycle path by architectural qualification
items.situation: A path is slow or crosses control logic, and the team wants a timing exception: reset paths, config paths, slow enables, pipelined buses, mode logic.
items.derivation: 1. Enumerate functional modes and prove whether launch and capture can ever occur with a same-cycle timing requirement. If no functional relationship exists, use a false path. 2. If the architecture intentionally allows N destination cycles, use a multicycle path: setup multicycle N. 3. Add the corresponding hold exception, usually N-1, to avoid making hold one cycle too strict; for N=2, set_multicycle_path 2 -setup and set_multicycle_path 1 -hold (confidence in the N-1 idiom 0.8). 4. Qualify the exception with mode pins, through points, or case conditions, then verify no bypass path defeats the qualification.
items.wrong_way: Declaring a false path because the path fails timing, or declaring a multicycle path without proving the enable/protocol actually spans N cycles. The silent break is loss of coverage: real functional paths are no longer checked, or hold becomes impossible because the hold exception was omitted.
items.defense: RTL waveforms showing the N-cycle enable, reset sequence, register write protocol, mode-pin truth table, and a search showing all alternate paths are qualified or excluded.
items.signoff_risk: Too broad: real timing relationships are unchecked and can cause functional corruption. Too narrow or missing: unnecessary timing failures and wasted fixing on architecturally relaxed paths.
items.node_era_note: no-era-difference-recalled

items.pattern_name: Asynchronous clock-domain boundary with controlled exceptions
items.situation: Two clock domains are unrelated in frequency or phase, and signals cross between them through synchronizers or handshakes.
items.derivation: 1. Prove the clocks are truly asynchronous: independent sources, unlocked PLLs, or no fixed divider/phase relationship. 2. At the domain boundary, remove meaningless setup/hold checks with set_clock_groups -asynchronous or equivalent false paths, but only after listing all crossing points. 3. Where a control path into a synchronizer needs bounded latency for protocol reasons, do not false-path that segment; constrain it with set_max_delay -datapath_only. A common budget is max_delay = N_resolve * T_dest - setup_dest - uncertainty_dest - margin M, where N_resolve is often 1 or 2 destination cycles (confidence 0.5) and M is often 5% to 10% of T_dest (confidence 0.4). 4. Keep destination-domain synchronizer flop-to-flop paths timed normally, and constrain asynchronous resets separately.
items.wrong_way: Blanket set_clock_groups between all clocks, including derived or phase-related clocks, or false-pathing CDC paths without checking that a synchronizer and handshake actually bound the transfer. This silently removes timing on paths that are synchronous or need a latency bound.
items.defense: Clock tree topology, PLL/divider analysis, CDC lint results, synchronizer schematic, and waveform or protocol proof that the crossing is asynchronous and resolved.
items.signoff_risk: Too loose: real synchronous paths or insufficient CDC latency are unchecked, causing metastability or protocol failure. Too tight: false failures on asynchronous paths and wasted fixing.
items.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below jitter and variation make synchronizer setup and resolution margins less forgiving than at 28nm

items.pattern_name: Pre-implementation interface budget allocation
items.situation: Two blocks have not yet been implemented, but floorplan and integration need boundary timing budgets to prevent later surprises.
items.derivation: 1. Start with period P, receiver setup S, and expected clock uncertainty U. 2. Estimate interconnect delay W from floorplan distance: W = length_est * wire_delay_per_mm, using historical order-of wire delay (confidence 0.4). 3. Reserve integration margin M, often 10% of P before floorplan matures (confidence 0.4). 4. Compute remaining slack R = P - S - U - W - M. 5. Split R between sender internal logic and receiver input logic; a common unknown split is 50/50 (confidence 0.3), or skew toward the more complex receiver. 6. Translate to SDC: at the sender output, set_output_delay max = W + receiver_budget + M, which leaves the sender internal budget as P - S - U - W - receiver_budget - M.
items.wrong_way: Using a fixed 50% period split with zero interconnect delay, or double-counting the same wire delay in both blocks. The silent break appears at integration: one block is blamed for a path that was impossible from the first budget.
items.defense: Floorplan distance, historical wire delay per mm, repeater plan, protocol latency, prior implementation data, and a written margin register that shows what was reserved and why.
items.signoff_risk: Too tight: blocks chase impossible boundary timing, causing schedule slip and over-optimization. Too loose: interface timing fails late, forcing expensive cross-block ECOs.
items.node_era_note: advanced nodes make wire and repeater estimates more uncertain, so early budgets need more frequent re-correlation than at 28nm

items.pattern_name: Stage margin and planned relaxation
items.situation: Early implementation has poor parasitics, no final clock tree, and unknown skew, but timing-driven implementation still needs targets.
items.derivation: 1. Estimate stage uncertainty: pre-route wire load, missing clock skew, extraction approximation. 2. Add setup margin M_stage, often 5% to 15% of period or order of 100ps for GHz-class clocks (confidence 0.4), via clock uncertainty, derate, or additional path margin. 3. Track timing correlation after each stage: post-CTS, post-route, extracted parasitics. 4. Relax the margin in steps matched to measured correlation, for example removing part after CTS when skew becomes real and more after final extraction (confidence in stepwise relaxation 0.35). 5. Stop relaxing only when signoff parasitics, corners, and clock models are frozen.
items.wrong_way: Leaving the early overconstraint in place at signoff, or relaxing it before real parasitics and clock skew exist. The first causes false failures and wasted fixing; the second allows implementation to converge to a design that later fails.
items.defense: Historical stage-to-signoff correlation data, slack trend reports, a named margin register, and explicit approval for each relaxation step.
items.signoff_risk: Too tight at signoff: false timing failures, unnecessary ECO, higher power/area. Too loose early: false convergence and late signoff timing escape.
items.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below extraction and variation uncertainty usually require more staged margin discipline than 28nm

items.pattern_name: Virtual clock for external or missing IO clock
items.situation: IO timing must be constrained against an external clock that does not exist as a net inside the block, or the board clock is not routed to the constrained boundary.
items.derivation: 1. Create a virtual clock with the external interface period P_ext. If duty cycle is unknown, assume 50% initially (confidence 0.5), then check edge-sensitive protocols for other waveform assumptions. 2. Derive phase offset from the protocol if specified; otherwise use conservative zero phase and verify both edge relationships if possible. 3. Apply set_input_delay or set_output_delay relative to the virtual clock using external timing specs: max = tco_max or equivalent + board/package delay_max + margin M; min = tco_min + board/package delay_min. M is often 5% of P_ext early (confidence 0.4). 4. If the internal sampling clock is different, explicitly constrain the relationship between the virtual clock and internal clock as asynchronous, source-synchronous, or max/min bounded.
items.wrong_way: Using an internal clock as if it were the external clock when phase, frequency, or jitter are not the same. This creates false synchronous timing relationships and can make signoff pass while the board interface fails.
items.defense: Protocol specification, external device datasheet, eye-diagram or timing-budget spreadsheet, board delay estimate, and explicit statement of why the virtual clock model matches the interface.
items.signoff_risk: Too tight: internal IO logic is over-optimized against a fictitious clock relationship. Too loose: real external timing problems are not checked and escape to board bring-up.

items.pattern_name: Generated/divided clock edge and latency derivation
items.situation: A clock is produced inside the design by a divider, mux, PLL output, or gated clock and must be constrained as a generated clock.
items.derivation: 1. Identify the master clock, division ratio or edge sequence, and the exact pin/net where the generated clock is defined. 2. For divide-by-N, the generated period is N * master_period; if duty cycle is not simple, specify explicit edges rather than only a divide factor (N from RTL is usually high confidence 0.8). 3. Include divider propagation latency in the generated clock path, either through the generated clock definition or by ensuring the divider cell delay is in the timing graph. 4. Decide master-to-generated relationship: if fixed phase, let timing checks relate edges; if the generated clock can be async or glitchy due to mux/reset, constrain the mux or add false/group exceptions only after proving no functional path.
items.wrong_way: Creating a generated clock with the wrong divide value or default waveform, or false-pathing master-to-divided clock paths because they look separate. The silent break is incorrect setup/hold relationships: paths may be checked against the wrong capture edge or not checked at all.
items.defense: RTL divider waveform, edge count, reset/mux behavior, clock topology diagram, and a check that the generated clock edges match simulation or static clock graph reports.
items.signoff_risk: Wrong period/phase too tight: false failures and useless fixing. Wrong period/phase too loose: real timing across divided or muxed clocks escapes to silicon.
items.node_era_note: no-era-difference-recalled

items.pattern_name: Asynchronous handshake latency budget
items.situation: A request/acknowledge, valid/ready, or FIFO interface crosses unrelated clock domains and timing cannot be checked as a normal synchronous path.
items.derivation: 1. Identify the handshake protocol and the minimum required pulse or acknowledge window in the destination domain. For a pulse crossing a two-flop synchronizer, the minimum width is often 2 destination cycles (confidence 0.5). 2. Bound the combinational delay into the first synchronizer flop: set_max_delay -datapath_only = min_window - setup_sync - uncertainty_dest - margin M, with M often 5% of destination period (confidence 0.4). 3. False-path or group the asynchronous relationship only for segments that are truly protocol-bounded; keep destination-domain synchronizer and logic paths timed normally. 4. For multibit handshakes, constrain relative bit skew or use Gray-coded pointers; the skew budget should be less than one destination cycle minus setup and margin (confidence 0.4).
items.wrong_way: False-pathing the entire handshake because it is asynchronous, without proving pulse width, synchronizer depth, or bit-skew behavior. The silent break is missed pulses, FIFO overflow/underflow, or sampling an invalid multibit value.
items.defense: Handshake protocol spec, FIFO/synchronizer design details, waveforms showing minimum pulse width, CDC lint structure checks, and proof that multibit transfers are Gray-coded or mux-synchronized.
items.signoff_risk: Too loose: asynchronous protocol failures that are invisible to ordinary timing signoff. Too tight: false timing failures on paths that are architecturally resolved by the handshake.
items.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below metastability and jitter make handshake pulse-width margins more important than at 28nm

items.pattern_name: Block-boundary input/output delay budgeting via period split
items.situation: Two blocks (or a block and top-level interconnect) are implemented separately and communicate synchronously across a boundary; each block's SDC needs input_delay/output_delay values before the other side exists in netlist form.
items.derivation: Start from the shared clock period T at the boundary. Subtract an estimated interconnect delay (wire + any boundary buffering) I, estimated early from floorplan wire-load or a placeholder (e.g. 10-15% of T for a typical reasonably-sized block-to-block wire). The remaining budget (T - I) is split between the launching block's internal output path and the receiving block's internal input path, often roughly proportional to each side's logic depth expectation, but a common starting split is 50/50 when no better info exists. So output_delay on the driving block's SDC = I + (share allocated to receive side), and input_delay on the receiving block's SDC reflects the same I plus driver-side share, expressed as 'time already consumed before this pin'. Iterating: as floorplan matures, replace the wire-load estimate with actual RC-extracted or global-route-estimated delay.
items.wrong_way: Giving both blocks the full period T as available budget without subtracting interconnect delay (i.e., forgetting interconnect is shared, not free), or worse, having each block's owner independently assume they get most of the period, causing double-booking. This silently breaks at integration when actual interconnect delay eats into both sides' assumed slack, and violations only appear at chip-level timing, far too late to easily fix.
items.defense: Point to the interconnect delay estimate's source (early floorplan wire-load model or a prior similar block's actual number), show the 50/50 or logic-depth-weighted split explicitly in a spreadsheet, and cross-check that summed input_delay + output_delay assumptions from both block owners equal (T - I), not more.
items.signoff_risk: Too tight (budget assumed smaller interconnect delay than reality): chip-level setup violations at the boundary that require late ECOs or spec relaxation. Too loose (budget over-allocated interconnect delay, starving block-internal budget less than needed): blocks close individually with margin to spare, wasting achievable frequency, discovered only when someone asks why the chip is slower than either block's standalone number.
items.node_era_note: at 7nm-and-below, interconnect delay is a much larger fraction of period than at 28nm, so the naive 50/50 split is less defensible and teams more often insist on an RC-based estimate even at floorplan stage
items._numeric_confidence_notes: assumes interconnect estimate around 10-15% of period as a common starting point (confidence 0.4); assumes 50/50 split as a common default absent better data (confidence 0.45)

items.pattern_name: False path vs multicycle path decision for slow/quasi-static control signals
items.situation: A path exists in the timing graph (e.g., a mode-select, configuration register, or reset synchronizer output feeding combinational logic) but the signal is known to change far less often than every clock cycle, and normal single-cycle timing would be needlessly hard or impossible to meet.
items.derivation: First determine whether the path is truly never required to be sampled correctly on the very next cycle after a change (justifies false_path) versus is allowed extra cycles but must still eventually be captured correctly within N cycles (justifies multicycle_path -setup N). The distinguishing question: does functional correctness ever depend on the receiving logic seeing the new value within a bounded number of cycles? If yes, use multicycle with N derived from the known minimum interval between legal changes of the source signal (e.g., a signal architecturally guaranteed to be stable for at least 4 cycles after any change becomes 'set_multicycle_path 4 -setup' with a corresponding 'set_multicycle_path 3 -hold' to keep the hold check aligned to the cycle before the new setup edge). If the path is fundamentally asynchronous or functionally irrelevant to timing (e.g., a scan/test-only path, or a signal whose value at the sampling edge genuinely never matters), false_path is used instead.
items.wrong_way: Applying false_path to a signal that actually does need to be captured within a bounded time (common shortcut to 'make timing pass'), which silently removes the path from all timing analysis so a real functional timing failure (data changing too close to a legitimate sample point) is never caught by STA and only shows up as an intermittent functional bug in silicon or emulation.
items.defense: Cite the RTL/microarchitectural guarantee (e.g., a documented minimum hold-time-in-cycles for the control signal, enforced by a counter or handshake in the design) as the basis for the multicycle N, and show the corresponding hold multicycle adjustment (N-1) was also applied so hold checking wasn't silently left at the default single-cycle hold window, which would over-constrain hold and cause unnecessary buffer insertion.
items.signoff_risk: Too tight (using single-cycle timing or too small an N when the real guarantee is looser): wastes implementation effort meeting an unnecessarily hard constraint, sometimes forcing pipeline stages that aren't functionally needed. Too loose (false_path where multicycle was appropriate, or N larger than the real guarantee): real setup/hold problems on that path are masked and can cause silicon failures that STA never flagged.
items.node_era_note: no-era-difference-recalled
items._numeric_confidence_notes: the example of 'stable for at least 4 cycles -> multicycle 4/3' is illustrative only (confidence 0.3 that this specific number pattern generalizes; the setup-N/hold-N-1 relationship itself is standard and confidence is higher, ~0.6)

items.pattern_name: Over-constraining (frequency margin) during early implementation
items.situation: Early in physical implementation (initial placement, early CTS), before parasitics and final library corners are accurate, teams often run timing at a tighter clock period than the actual target to build in margin against later degradation.
items.derivation: Take the true target period T_target and apply a margin percentage M (commonly discussed in the range of 5-10% early on, sometimes more at very early floorplan stages) to get the working period used in early optimization: T_work = T_target * (1 - M). As the design matures (post-route, signoff parasitics available, real OCV/derate applied), M is reduced stage by stage until T_work converges to T_target (or slightly above it, since some residual margin is normal even at final signoff).
items.wrong_way: Keeping the same large early-stage margin all the way through to signoff without relaxing it, which silently wastes area/power (cells oversized, extra buffering) chasing a target no longer necessary, or conversely relaxing the margin too early (before parasitics are trustworthy) so the design looks like it's closing timing when in fact later corners will blow through the true target once real interconnect delay is added.
items.defense: Show the margin-reduction schedule tied to specific implementation milestones (e.g., 'margin relaxed only after post-route parasitics extracted, not before'), and present trend data of slack at each stage to justify that the margin was earning real protection against known sources of change (OCV widening, layer assignment, clock tree insertion) rather than being an arbitrary number.
items.signoff_risk: Too tight (margin never relaxed): area/power penalty and possibly missed schedule chasing an artificially hard target. Too loose (margin removed too early or too small from the start): signoff timing violations appear late when the real corners and parasitics are in, often surfacing after the design was believed closed, forcing late ECOs under schedule pressure.
items.node_era_note: at 7nm-and-below, the gap between early-stage and signoff-stage estimates is typically larger due to increased variation and multi-corner/multi-mode complexity, so margin schedules tend to be more conservative and staged more finely than at 28nm
items._numeric_confidence_notes: assumes 5-10% early margin as a commonly recalled starting range (confidence 0.4)

items.pattern_name: Virtual clock definition for primary I/O timing
items.situation: A block's inputs or outputs are timed relative to an external device or another chip whose internal clock structure is not part of this block's netlist (e.g., a chip-level I/O interface), so there's no physical clock object in this block to reference for input_delay/output_delay.
items.derivation: Define a virtual clock (create_clock with no -add to any real pin, just a name) with the same period and, critically, the same relationship (edge alignment/phase) as the external device's clock is specified to have relative to this chip's I/O clock. input_delay and output_delay values are then set relative to this virtual clock, using the external device's specified setup/hold or valid-delay windows (from its datasheet or interface spec) translated into the input_delay/output_delay arithmetic: for an input, input_delay = external device's clock-to-out max delay + board/trace delay; for an output, output_delay = external receiving device's required setup time + board/trace delay.
items.wrong_way: Reusing the block's internal core clock object directly as if it were the interface clock without checking whether the actual I/O clock has different phase alignment or period (e.g., due to PLL phase shift or a different divide ratio), which silently mis-times every I/O path relative to the real external timing relationship and is often only caught in board bring-up, not simulation or STA.
items.defense: Reference the interface specification document's timing diagram directly (datasheet setup/hold or valid-delay numbers) as the source of the input_delay/output_delay arithmetic, and show that the virtual clock's period/edges match the documented external clock relationship, not an assumption.
items.signoff_risk: Too tight (input_delay/output_delay assumed worse external timing than actual): wastes internal timing budget, potentially forcing unnecessary pipeline stages on I/O paths. Too loose (assumed better external timing than actual, e.g., ignoring board trace delay): real interface timing failures only appear at board bring-up since STA showed the path passing.

items._numeric_confidence_notes: no specific numbers asserted beyond the general arithmetic shape

items.pattern_name: Generated/divided clock constraint derivation
items.situation: A clock is produced inside the design by dividing or gating a root clock (e.g., a simple toggle flip-flop divider or clock-gating cell producing a slower derived clock domain) and STA needs a correct create_generated_clock rather than an independent create_clock that could desynchronize from the source.
items.derivation: Use create_generated_clock referencing the source clock pin and the actual divide/multiply relationship implemented in the divider logic (e.g., -divide_by 2 for a simple toggle divider), applied at the output pin of the generating register/cell, so the tool derives the generated clock's period, waveform, and phase alignment automatically from the source clock rather than being independently specified. Verify the generated clock's edges align with the expected functional behavior of the divider (e.g., confirming which edge of the source clock the divided clock toggles on) by checking the divider's actual logic, not assuming a textbook 50% duty cycle divider.
items.wrong_way: Defining the divided clock as an independent create_clock with a manually computed period, which loses the phase/edge relationship to the source clock entirely; this silently makes the tool treat the two clock domains as unrelated (effectively asynchronous) for timing purposes, so crossing paths between the root clock and the derived clock get analyzed with incorrect (often overly pessimistic or, if false-pathed, dangerously optimistic) skew assumptions instead of the true, tool-derivable relationship.
items.defense: Show the divider RTL/schematic and confirm the create_generated_clock's -divide_by (or -multiply_by) and -edges settings match the actual logic implementation, and demonstrate in the generated clock's reported waveform (from the tool) that it matches the expected functional divided waveform.
items.signoff_risk: Too tight/wrong relationship (e.g., wrong edge assumed): paths between root and divided domain may show false violations that get incorrectly 'fixed' by adding unnecessary margin or exceptions, or conversely real violations get masked because the tool thinks the domains are unrelated. Too loose (treating as fully asynchronous when it's not): crossing paths lose the benefit of the known, analyzable relationship and either get over-margined (wasting timing) or under-constrained if someone false-paths them assuming asynchrony that doesn't actually exist.
items.node_era_note: no-era-difference-recalled

items.pattern_name: Asynchronous clock-domain-crossing (CDC) constraint via false_path plus synchronizer awareness
items.situation: A signal crosses from one clock domain to a genuinely unrelated (asynchronous) clock domain through a synchronizer (e.g., a 2-flop synchronizer chain), and the path between the two domains needs an SDC exception since no valid static timing relationship exists between the clocks.
items.derivation: Apply set_false_path (or set_clock_groups -asynchronous for the whole domain pair, if broader) specifically from the synchronizer's first-stage input to its capturing flop, so STA does not attempt to compute a meaningless setup/hold check across unrelated clocks. Critically, the false_path (or async group) is scoped as narrowly as possible -- typically just the crossing point itself -- so that all other timing within each domain (including from the synchronizer's output onward) remains fully and normally checked; the exception must not accidentally blanket-cover logic that is not actually part of the crossing.
items.wrong_way: Applying a broad set_clock_groups -asynchronous between the two entire clock domains (rather than scoping to just the crossing flops) when there are actually other legitimate, related paths between those domains elsewhere in the design (e.g., a shared reset tree or a second, intentionally synchronous path), which silently removes real timing checks on paths that do need them, masking genuine violations elsewhere in the two domains' interaction.
items.defense: Point to the synchronizer's schematic/RTL showing it is a proper multi-flop synchronizer (not a single flop, which would be a metastability/CDC design bug independent of SDC), and show the false_path/async-group scoping is limited to exactly the crossing pins, verified by checking the SDC exception report for unintended path coverage.
items.signoff_risk: Too broad an exception (covers more than the true crossing): real synchronous paths elsewhere between the domains lose timing coverage, and violations there go undetected until functional failure. Missing or too narrow an exception (crossing not excepted at all): STA reports a spurious, unfixable 'violation' on an inherently asynchronous path, which teams sometimes 'fix' by adding meaningless buffering that does nothing for actual metastability risk (which is a separate CDC/MTBF concern, not a static timing one).

items.pattern_name: Interconnect budgeting between two not-yet-implemented blocks using a placeholder wire-load/RC estimate
items.situation: At RTL/early floorplan stage, two blocks that will eventually be connected through top-level routing need boundary timing constraints (input_delay/output_delay) before either block or the top-level interconnect has real layout.
items.derivation: Estimate interconnect delay using a rough distance-based or wire-load-model-based number derived from the expected floorplan (e.g., block A and B are expected to be roughly adjacent vs across the die), producing a placeholder delay value I_est. This I_est is subtracted from the shared period the same way as boundary budgeting (see the period-split pattern), but flagged explicitly as provisional pending floorplan. A tracking mechanism (e.g., a budget spreadsheet or comment in the SDC) records the assumption so it can be revisited once floorplan or global-route estimates are available.
items.wrong_way: Treating the early placeholder I_est as final and never revisiting it once real floorplan/placement data exists, so if the actual distance between the blocks turns out much larger than assumed (e.g., a late floorplan change moves one block across the die), the boundary timing silently becomes wrong and isn't caught until block-level or chip-level signoff, by which point both blocks may have already been 'closed' to the wrong budget.
items.defense: Show the placeholder estimate is explicitly labeled provisional and tied to a specific floorplan assumption (e.g., 'assumes blocks share an edge'), with a defined checkpoint (e.g., 'to be revisited at floorplan freeze') rather than presented as a firm number.
items.signoff_risk: Too tight (I_est assumed larger than reality): blocks over-budget for interconnect, individually closing with unnecessary margin, wasted effort. Too loose (I_est assumed smaller than the eventual real distance): chip-level integration reveals a boundary timing violation that neither block owner expected, often discovered late and expensive to fix since both blocks were independently signed off against the wrong assumption.
items.node_era_note: at 7nm-and-below, placeholder interconnect estimates are far riskier because wire delay is proportionally larger and less linear with distance, so teams more often insist on at least a rough global-route-based estimate rather than a pure wire-load-model guess even at early stages
items._numeric_confidence_notes: no specific numeric margin asserted; pattern is about process/tracking discipline rather than a specific arithmetic constant

items.pattern_name: Hierarchical block input-delay budget from unimplemented launch block
items.situation: Two blocks A and B in same clock domain; B has input port driven by A; A not yet implemented; need set_input_delay on B's input so B's implementation leaves enough margin for A to be built later.
items.derivation: Assume clock period T = 10ns (confidence 0.2 — example only). Budget split: launch logic (A internal) = 0.50  T = 5ns (confidence 0.4 on 50% split), interconnect/wire delay = 0.10  T = 1ns (confidence 0.4 on 10% interconnect), capture internal (B input-to-flop) = 0.40  T = 4ns (confidence 0.4 on 40% capture). set_input_delay -clock clk [get_ports IN] value = launch + interconnect = 0.60  T = 6ns. Remaining time for B's internal logic = T - input_delay - T_setup = 4ns - T_setup. If A later requires more than 5ns, B's budget is already consumed and integration fails.
items.wrong_way: Setting input_delay = T (period) leaves 0ns for B internal logic — always fails STA. Setting input_delay = 0 leaves full period for B but A can never meet its launch delay in integration. Silently breaks: over-constrained B wastes area/power; under-constrained B passes STA but system fails at integration.
items.defense: Engineer presents the budget spreadsheet showing the 50/10/40 split justified by pipeline stage count and wire-load estimates from similar blocks; claims this is conservative for A's complexity.
items.signoff_risk: Too tight: B over-optimized, wasted power/area, possible failure to close timing. Too loose: A cannot meet launch delay at integration, system timing failure on silicon.
items.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below: OCV/POCV requires extra 10-15% margin in budget split (confidence 0.6), reducing the capture-side allocation

items.pattern_name: False path vs multicycle on slow control/configuration registers
items.situation: Configuration or reset signal that changes only at boot or infrequently; crosses flops in same clock domain but data is not required to be valid next cycle.
items.derivation: If signal only needs to propagate in N cycles (e.g., N=2 for a two-cycle config write), set_multicycle_path N -from [src_regs] -to [dest_regs]. For same-clock slow control, set_multicycle_path 2. Hold check defaults to same edge; add set_multicycle_path 1 -hold to keep hold check at launch edge. Arithmetic: setup check moves to cycle N, so required time = N*T - T_setup. If truly async and never timed (e.g., test reset), set_false_path -from [src] -to [dest].
items.wrong_way: Setting set_false_path on a signal that actually changes at operational speed — silently breaks: chip works at low speed or in simulation but fails intermittently at target frequency because data arrives late relative to capture edge.
items.defense: Engineer shows waveform or protocol spec proving signal only toggles once per N cycles; points to RTL state machine guaranteeing N-cycle separation.
items.signoff_risk: Too tight (no exception): wasted effort fixing unneeded paths, area/power penalty. Too loose (false path when multicycle needed): data corruption if signal changes faster than assumed; intermittent system failure.
items.node_era_note: no-era-difference-recalled

items.pattern_name: Early-implementation over-constraint margin
items.situation: Block synthesis or pre-CTS, before final clock tree and routing; want margin so later stages don't invalidate timing closure.
items.derivation: Target clock period = T. Set constraint to 0.80  T (i.e., 20% margin) (confidence 0.5 on 20% being typical; some teams use 10-15%). Alternatively, set_clock_uncertainty additional 0.05  T (confidence 0.5 on 5% extra). Arithmetic: if T=5ns, constrain to 4ns. Relax to T after CTS or route. Over-constraint removed in final signoff constraint set.
items.wrong_way: Over-constraining by 50% (0.5*T) — tool cannot close timing, wasted iterations, team blames flow. Or forgetting to relax before tapeout — chip ships over-margined, wasted power/area, no benefit.
items.defense: Engineer cites historical data from prior tapeouts showing post-CTS insertion delay consumed 15-20% of period (confidence 0.5); margin chosen to absorb this.
items.signoff_risk: Too tight: area/power penalty, possible failure to close timing, schedule slip. Too loose (no margin): post-P&R timing fails, late ECO required, tapeout delay.
items.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below: over-constrain by less (e.g., 10%) because tool has harder time closing on aggressive targets due to wire delay dominance (confidence 0.55)

items.pattern_name: Virtual clock for external-device input timing
items.situation: Chip receives data from external device with known t_co, board trace delay; need to constrain input port relative to external clock.
items.derivation: Create virtual clock: create_clock -name vclk -period T. set_input_delay -clock vclk -max t_co_ext + t_board_delay [get_ports IN]. Assume T=10ns (confidence 0.2), t_co_ext=2ns (confidence 0.3), t_board=1ns (confidence 0.3). Input delay = 3ns. Required internal arrival = T - input_delay - T_setup = 10 - 3 - 0.1 = 6.9ns for internal logic.
items.wrong_way: Using real internal clock with offset instead of virtual clock — creates false clock relationship, breaks timing analysis. Ignoring board delay — silently breaks: STA passes but system fails at board level because trace delay was not accounted.
items.defense: Engineer presents external device datasheet t_co max, board stack-up trace delay estimate, and system-level timing budget showing the arithmetic.
items.signoff_risk: Too tight: STA fails unnecessarily, over-design of input buffer. Too loose: system integration failure, external device setup not met at board level.
items.node_era_note: no-era-difference-recalled

items.pattern_name: Generated clock from divider for low-power domain
items.situation: Internal divided clock from PLL or RTL divider for a slower domain; need to constrain paths through divided clock and crossings back to fast domain.
items.derivation: create_generated_clock -name clk_div2 -source [master_pin] -divide_by 2 [divider_output]. Period of clk_div2 = 2*T. For paths from fast to slow domain: launch period = T, capture period = 2T. Default setup check at first slow-clock edge (T) may be too tight; often set_multicycle_path 2 -to [slow_domain_regs] to allow full 2T. Arithmetic: if T=5ns, fast-to-slow default setup check at 5ns; with multicycle 2, check at 10ns.
items.wrong_way: Using create_clock instead of create_generated_clock — breaks clock relationship, timing engine treats as async, no cross-domain paths analyzed. Silently breaks: paths between domains either falsely pass (no check) or are over-constrained.
items.defense: Engineer shows clock tree schematic, divider ratio, and cross-domain path report proving correct clock relationship and multicycle exception.
items.signoff_risk: Wrong command or missing multicycle: complete loss of valid timing checks or false violations; silicon failure if critical path escapes.
items.node_era_note: no-era-difference-recalled

items.pattern_name: Asynchronous CDC handshake max-delay constraint for MTBF
items.situation: Two async clock domains with handshake; clocks unrelated; need to bound metastability probability with max-delay on synchronizer flops.
items.derivation: set_clock_groups -asynchronous -group {clkA} -group {clkB}. For synchronizer flops, set_max_delay 0.5 * T_fast (confidence 0.4 on 0.5 factor; typical range 0.3-0.7). If T_fast=2ns, max_delay=1ns. This bounds the time for signal to propagate through first sync flop, reducing metastability window. Arithmetic: MTBF ∝ exp(delay/metastability_time_constant); tighter max_delay improves MTBF.
items.wrong_way: No constraint at all — no MTBF check, potential for rare metastability failures in field. Silently breaks: chip passes STA but fails intermittently in system due to unresolved CDC.
items.defense: Engineer presents MTBF calculation spreadsheet showing max_delay value achieves target MTBF (e.g., >1 year mean time between failures) given process metastability parameters.
items.signoff_risk: Too tight: routing congestion, wasted resources on short paths. Too loose: metastability not bounded, system fails intermittently; field returns.
items.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below: smaller nodes have smaller metastability window, so max_delay needs to be tighter (e.g., 0.3*T_fast, confidence 0.6); POCV also affects MTBF calculation

items.pattern_name: Clock uncertainty budgeting for PLL jitter and variation
items.situation: Setting clock_uncertainty for setup/hold to account for PLL jitter, AOCV/POCV, and clock-tree variation at various implementation stages.
items.derivation: Uncertainty = PLL_jitter + variation_margin. Assume PLL_jitter = 0.05  T (confidence 0.5 on 5%), AOCV_margin = 0.02  T (confidence 0.5 on 2%). Total = 0.07  T. For T=5ns, uncertainty = 0.35ns. Applied via set_clock_uncertainty 0.35 [get_clocks clk]. Pre-CTS: add estimated clock skew (e.g., 0.10T, confidence 0.4). Post-CTS: remove skew, keep jitter + variation.
items.wrong_way: Setting uncertainty = 0 — no margin for jitter; silicon fails at speed. Setting too high (e.g., 0.3*T) — cannot close timing, wasted area/power. Silently breaks: wrong uncertainty hides real timing problems or creates false failures.
items.defense: Engineer presents PLL datasheet jitter spec, process variation model (AOCV/POCV derate tables), and clock-tree insertion-delay estimate to justify the split.
items.signoff_risk: Too tight: fails STA, over-design. Too loose: silicon timing failure, chip doesn't meet frequency rating.
items.node_era_note: 7nm-and-below: POCV adds significant uncertainty, typically 2-3x 28nm (confidence 0.6), requiring higher budget or statistical timing

items.pattern_name: Output delay budget to external device
items.situation: Chip outputs data to external device with known t_su and board trace delay; need set_output_delay to constrain internal logic.
items.derivation: Create virtual clock vclk with period T. set_output_delay -clock vclk -max T - t_su_ext - t_board_delay [get_ports OUT]. Assume T=10ns (confidence 0.2), t_su_ext=1ns (confidence 0.3), t_board=0.5ns (confidence 0.3). Output_delay = 10 - 1 - 0.5 = 8.5ns. Internal logic must produce data 8.5ns after clock edge. Slack = T - output_delay - T_internal_delay - T_skew.
items.wrong_way: Setting output_delay = 0 — internal logic gets full period but external device misses data because t_su not accounted. Silently breaks: STA passes, board-level system fails.
items.defense: Engineer presents external device t_su spec, board trace delay calculation, and system timing budget showing the subtraction arithmetic.
items.signoff_risk: Too tight: internal logic over-optimized, power/area wasted. Too loose: external device setup violation at system level, board failure.
